### equate.evaluate.bcubed(pred_labels, true_labels)

B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.

Per record: precision is the share of its predicted cluster that truly belongs with
it, recall the share of its true cluster that the prediction kept with it; both are
averaged over records.

```pycon
>>> s = bcubed([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1])
>>> round(s.precision, 3), round(s.recall, 3)
(0.75, 0.667)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

### equate.evaluate.benchmark_matcher(matcher=None, , on=('toy_names',), n_seeds=3, ratios=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), fit=None, split='auto', ci='auto', n_boot=1000, ci_seed=0)

Score `matcher` on unseen-entity test splits of each benchmark in `on`.

`matcher(a, b)` returns `(i, j)` pairs (a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching)
qualifies); the default is `equate.match()`. `on` is a benchmark name, a
[`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.Benchmark), or an iterable of either. Scores are pairwise; a seed whose test
part has no gold pair is skipped with a warning, and a benchmark with no scorable
seed is an error. For each of `n_seeds` seeds the records of `a + b`
are split by entity (`ratios` = train/val/test); only the **test** part is
matched and scored, so a test entity was never seen in training.

`fit(train_a, train_b, train_pairs, val_a, val_b, val_pairs) -> matcher` makes the
harness train per seed: it gets the train and validation parts only (the split is
asserted leak-free first), and the matcher it returns is scored on test. Choose a
threshold on the validation part there ([`select_threshold()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.select_threshold)),
never on test.

`split` chooses the parts: `'entity'` is the seeded entity split above;
`'canonical'` uses the benchmark’s own `splits` (one run, `n_seeds` and
`ratios` ignored; no entity-leakage assertion, since a suite’s *seen-entity*
variants share entities across parts by design); `'auto'` (default) is canonical
when the benchmark has `splits`, else entity.

`ci` adds a **bootstrap confidence interval** to each row (doc 14 §7.4): the test
*entities* are resampled `n_boot` times (a cluster bootstrap: an entity’s pairs move
together) and the percentile interval of precision, recall and F1 is kept in
`BenchmarkRow.ci`. `'auto'` (default) computes a 95 % interval only for a
single-run benchmark — a canonical split has no seed spread, and a 500-pair test set
leaves a few points of F1 within noise; a level (`0.9`) computes it for every row;
`None` never. The resampling is seeded (`ci_seed`), so a report is reproducible.
A percentile interval cannot show uncertainty at a 0/1 boundary: a perfect run reads
`1.000 [1.000, 1.000]` — that is “no resample found an error”, not certainty.

```pycon
>>> report = benchmark_matcher(n_seeds=2)
>>> s = report.summary()['toy_names']
>>> s['f1'][0] > 0.8, s['n_seeds']
(True, 2)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`BenchmarkReport`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.BenchmarkReport)

### equate.evaluate.blocking_metrics(candidate_pairs, true_pairs, , n_a, n_b=None)

Return `{pair_completeness, reduction_ratio, pairs_quality, n_candidates}`.

- **pair_completeness (PC)** = `|candidates ∩ true| / |true|` — blocking *recall*
  (upper-bounds end-to-end recall);
- **reduction_ratio (RR)** = `1 - |candidates| / |all pairs|` — how much blocking pruned;
- **pairs_quality (PQ)** = `|candidates ∩ true| / |candidates|` — blocking *precision*.

`n_b=None` means a self-join (dedup) over `n_a` items, so
`|all pairs| = n_a*(n_a-1)/2`; otherwise `|all pairs| = n_a*n_b`. For a self-join,
pairs are canonicalized to unordered `(min, max)` so orientation doesn’t matter and
`(i, j)` / `(j, i)` count once. Empty `true_pairs` yields `pair_completeness=1.0`
(vacuously perfect recall); `reduction_ratio` is clamped to `[0, 1]`.

```pycon
>>> m = blocking_metrics([(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)], n_a=3, n_b=3)
>>> round(m['pair_completeness'], 2), round(m['pairs_quality'], 2)
(0.67, 1.0)
```

### equate.evaluate.bootstrap_ci(pred, gold, left_entities, , level=0.95, n_boot=1000, seed=0)

Percentile bootstrap interval of pairwise precision, recall and F1.

`pred` / `gold` are `(i, j)` pairs; `left_entities[i]` is the entity of left
record `i`. Entities (not pairs) are resampled with replacement and each pair is
weighted by how often its **left** record’s entity was drawn, so the pairs of one
entity succeed or fail together (a false positive counts against the entity of its
left record; entities with no left record in the test part are not resampled).

A resample with no predicted pair has no precision, and one with no gold pair no
recall: those resamples are left out of that metric’s interval (scoring them 1.0, as
[`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.Scores) does for a whole empty run, would inflate it). An
interval with no valid resample is `(nan, nan)`. Returns `{'precision': (lo,
hi), 'recall': ..., 'f1': ...}`. Memory is bounded: resamples are drawn in chunks.

```pycon
>>> ci = bootstrap_ci({(0, 0), (1, 1)}, {(0, 0), (1, 2)}, ['e0', 'e1'], n_boot=200)
>>> ci['precision'][0] <= 0.5 <= ci['precision'][1]
True
```

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### equate.evaluate.ceaf(pred_labels, true_labels, , variant='entity', matcher='optimal')

CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters.

`variant='entity'` (CEAF-e, φ4) weighs each aligned pair by
`2|K∩R| / (|K|+|R|)` and normalises by the number of clusters;
`variant='mention'` (CEAF-m, φ3) weighs by `|K∩R|` and normalises by the
number of records. The alignment is a maximum-weight assignment, resolved through
equate’s [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers) registry (`matcher`), never a
private Hungarian.

```pycon
>>> round(ceaf([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1]).f1, 3)
0.733
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

### equate.evaluate.cluster_metrics(pred_labels, true_labels, , backend='auto')

B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness.

`backend='auto'` uses `sklearn.metrics` for ARI / V-measure when sklearn is
installed and the numpy implementations otherwise; `'numpy'` forces the latter,
`'sklearn'` requires the former. The two agree; the choice only exists so the
core install needs neither.

```pycon
>>> m = cluster_metrics([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1], backend='numpy')
>>> sorted(m)
['ari', 'b3_f1', 'b3_precision', 'b3_recall', 'ceaf_e_f1', 'completeness',
 'homogeneity', 'v_measure']
```

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n_a, n_b)

Labels over `A + B` (B’s records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs.

The bridge from a matching between two collections to the entity view a cluster
metric or an entity split needs.

```pycon
>>> cross_pairs_to_labels([(0, 1)], n_a=2, n_b=2)
[0, 1, 2, 0]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

### equate.evaluate.data_dir()

The default root of the benchmark cache (not created until something is written).

* **Return type:**
  [`Path`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.Path)

### equate.evaluate.dblp_acm(\*\*config)

DBLP-ACM: 2616 × 2294 publications, 2224 matches (Leipzig; easy).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### equate.evaluate.default_store()

The default benchmark cache: a [`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.FileStore) over [`data_dir()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.data_dir).

* **Return type:**
  [`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.FileStore)

### equate.evaluate.difficulty_profile(a, b, gold)

`{'linearity', 'level', 'base_rate', 'n_a', 'n_b', 'n_gold'}` for a matching task.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### equate.evaluate.entity_split(entity_ids, , ratios=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), seed=0)

Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.

`entity_ids[i]` is record `i`’s true entity (e.g. from
[`cross_pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels) over a two-table gold matching).
Entities, not records, are shuffled (`seed`) and cut by `ratios`, so the parts
are disjoint in entities and roughly — not exactly — proportional in records.

```pycon
>>> s = entity_split([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], seed=1)
>>> assert_no_leakage([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], s.train, s.test)
>>> sorted(s.train + s.val + s.test) == list(range(10))
True
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.Split)

### equate.evaluate.fetch(key, source, , store=None, download=True, get=None)

The bytes of `source`, from `store` if cached, else downloaded and cached.

The bytes are checked against `source.sha256` **every time**, cached or not: a
cached copy that no longer matches (corrupted on disk, or a pin updated for a
re-issued file) is downloaded again; a download that does not match raises
`ValueError` and nothing is written. With `download=False` a missing or stale
key raises `FileNotFoundError` instead of reaching the network. `get(url) ->
bytes` is the downloader (default `http_get()`).

* **Return type:**
  [`bytes`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#bytes)

### equate.evaluate.gmd(pred_labels, true_labels, \*, merge_cost=<function unit_cost>, split_cost=<function unit_cost>)

Generalized merge distance: the cost of the splits and merges that turn the
predicted clustering into the true one (Menestrina, Whang & Garcia-Molina, VLDB 2010).

`split_cost(x, y)` prices splitting a cluster of `x + y` records into `x` and
`y`; `merge_cost(x, y)` merging an `x`- and a `y`-record cluster. The defaults
([`unit_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.unit_cost)) count operations; [`pair_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.pair_cost) for both gives the pairwise
error count; [`linear_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.linear_cost) `(k1, k2)` is `k1 + k2·x·y`. Unlike F-measures it
is a distance (`0` = identical), and its costs let an application say whether a
wrong merge hurts more than a missed one. Linear time.

As in the paper, this is the cost of the *legal* path — split each predicted cluster
along the true clusters, then merge the pieces of each true cluster — and the costs
must be **operation-order independent** (constant, `k·x·y`, or `k1 + k2·x·y`):
for other costs the result can depend on the labels’ names. With unit costs a path
that merges first can occasionally be cheaper; GMD is defined as the legal path.

```pycon
>>> gmd([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1])   # split {2, 3}, merge {2} into {0, 1}
2.0
>>> gmd([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1], merge_cost=pair_cost, split_cost=pair_cost)
3.0
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.labels_to_pairs(labels)

Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.

```pycon
>>> sorted(labels_to_pairs([0, 0, 1, 0]))
[(0, 1), (0, 3), (1, 3)]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`set`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#set)[[`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int), [`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]]

### equate.evaluate.linear_cost(k1=0.0, k2=1.0)

A cost `k1 + k2 * x * y` — the order-independent family GMD is defined for.

```pycon
>>> linear_cost(1, 0)(3, 4), linear_cost(0, 1)(3, 4)
(1.0, 12.0)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)

### equate.evaluate.linearity(a, b, gold, , max_pairs=10000000)

Best pairwise F1 of a single threshold on TF-IDF cosine similarity over `a × b`.

Records (mappings) are compared through their joined values. Ties are cut together
(a threshold cannot split equal scores). `0.0` when there is nothing to find.
Every pair is scored densely (peak ~130 bytes per pair), so inputs over `max_pairs`
pairs raise `ValueError` rather than exhaust memory; raise the limit knowingly.

```pycon
>>> round(linearity(['apple pie', 'kiwi'], ['kiwi', 'apple pie'], {(0, 1), (1, 0)}), 2)
1.0
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.list_benchmarks()

Names of the registered benchmarks.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]

### equate.evaluate.load_benchmark(name, \*\*config)

Build a registered benchmark (`config` goes to its loader).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### equate.evaluate.pair_cost(x, y)

Cost `x * y`: the record pairs a split separates or a merge joins — with it,
GMD equals the number of pairwise errors (false positives + false negatives).

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n)

Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.

Labels are canonical: numbered in order of each cluster’s smallest record, so two
pair sets that induce the same partition give equal label lists. A record no pair
mentions is a singleton.

```pycon
>>> pairs_to_labels([(0, 1), (1, 2), (4, 5)], n=6)
[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

### equate.evaluate.pairwise_prf(pred_pairs, true_pairs, , self_join=False)

Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.

`self_join=True` (deduplication within one collection) treats `(i, j)` and
`(j, i)` as one pair and drops `(i, i)`; otherwise pairs are `(row of A, row
of B)` and orientation matters.

```pycon
>>> s = pairwise_prf([(0, 0), (1, 2)], [(0, 0), (1, 1)])
>>> s.precision, s.recall, s.support
(0.5, 0.5, 2)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

### equate.evaluate.pr_auc(scores, y_true)

Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.

Records with tied scores enter the ranking together (one threshold step), so the
figure does not depend on the input order of ties. No positives → `nan`.

```pycon
>>> round(pr_auc([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.1], [1, 0, 1, 0]), 3)
0.833
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.ranking_metrics(ranked, gold, , ks=(1, 5, 10))

Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.

`ranked[q]` is query `q`’s candidates, best first; `gold[q]` is its true match
or a collection of them. Queries with no gold are skipped; a query whose gold never
appears contributes 0.

```pycon
>>> m = ranking_metrics({'a': ['x', 'y'], 'b': ['z', 'w']}, {'a': 'y', 'b': 'z'}, ks=(1,))
>>> m['recall_at_1'], m['mrr']
(0.5, 0.75)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### equate.evaluate.select_threshold(scores, y_true, , optimize='f1')

The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`.

Pass **validation** scores and labels. `optimize` is `'f1'`, `'precision'` or
`'recall'`; ties go to the higher threshold (fewer predicted matches). Returns the
threshold and the [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.Scores) it achieves on the data it was chosen on — which
are therefore optimistic, and are not a test result.

```pycon
>>> t, s = select_threshold([0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3], [1, 1, 0, 1])
>>> t, round(s.f1, 3)
(0.3, 0.857)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float), [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)]

### equate.evaluate.subset_pairs(gold, rows_a, rows_b)

Gold pairs with both ends in the subset, re-indexed into the subset.

```pycon
>>> sorted(subset_pairs({(0, 1), (2, 0)}, [2, 0], [0, 1]))
[(0, 0), (1, 1)]
```

### equate.evaluate.unit_cost(x, y)

Cost 1 per split or merge, whatever the sizes (GMD counts operations).

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.wdc_products(, corner_cases=80, unseen=100, dev_size='large', seed=0, store=None, download=True, get=None, verify=True, profile=True)

WDC Products as a two-table benchmark with its canonical train/valid/test split.

The defaults pick the hardest generalization variant — 80 % corner cases, every test
entity unseen in training (research doc 14, §7.6) — with the large development set.
Gold pairs every `a`/`b` offer of the same product, across parts too (a seen test
product matches its training offers); only the test-part gold is scored. Row order
within each part is shuffled with `seed`. `meta['leakage']` counts test offers
that also appear, identically, in train or valid. WDC’s own files have such overlap:
hundreds in the 50 %-unseen variants, a few in valid for 0 %. A warning says so.

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### Modules

| [`suites`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.suites)         | Loaders for the standard matching benchmarks, fetched on first use into a store.        |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.benchmark)   | Self-benchmarking: a benchmark registry and an honest-by-default harness.               |
| [`difficulty`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.difficulty.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.difficulty) | How hard is a benchmark? A measured difficulty profile to print next to a score.        |
| [`labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.labels)         | Convert between the two granularities: pairs and cluster labels.                        |
| [`metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.metrics)       | Pairwise and cluster-level match metrics, dependency-light.                             |
| [`ranking`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.ranking)       | Threshold-free and ranking metrics, and threshold selection as its own step.            |
| [`scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.scores)         | The one score type every metric returns: precision and recall, never F1 alone.          |
| [`split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.split)           | Leakage-aware splitting: split over entities, so test entities are unseen.              |
| [`store`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#module-equate.evaluate.store)           | Where downloaded benchmark data lives: a store (a `MutableMapping`), never the package. |


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md

# equate.evaluate.labels

Convert between the two granularities: pairs and cluster labels.

Pairwise metrics take pair sets; cluster metrics take a label per record. The
conversion is a deliberate act (research doc 14, §2.2): [`pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.pairs_to_labels) takes
the **transitive closure** of a pair set (union-find), which can merge records a matcher
never linked directly, so a user who evaluates a 1:1 matcher with a cluster metric sees
exactly what they are asking for.

### Functions

| [`cross_pairs_to_labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.cross_pairs_to_labels)(pairs, \*, n_a, n_b)   | Labels over `A + B` (B's records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs.   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`labels_to_pairs`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.labels_to_pairs)(labels)                      | Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.                                   |
| [`pairs_to_labels`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.labels.html.md#equate.evaluate.labels.pairs_to_labels)(pairs, \*, n)                | Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.          |

### equate.evaluate.labels.cross_pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n_a, n_b)

Labels over `A + B` (B’s records offset by `n_a`) from two-table `(i, j)` pairs.

The bridge from a matching between two collections to the entity view a cluster
metric or an entity split needs.

```pycon
>>> cross_pairs_to_labels([(0, 1)], n_a=2, n_b=2)
[0, 1, 2, 0]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]

### equate.evaluate.labels.labels_to_pairs(labels)

Every within-cluster pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`.

```pycon
>>> sorted(labels_to_pairs([0, 0, 1, 0]))
[(0, 1), (0, 3), (1, 3)]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`set`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#set)[[`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int), [`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]]

### equate.evaluate.labels.pairs_to_labels(pairs, , n)

Cluster label per record `0..n-1` from the transitive closure of `pairs`.

Labels are canonical: numbered in order of each cluster’s smallest record, so two
pair sets that induce the same partition give equal label lists. A record no pair
mentions is a singleton.

```pycon
>>> pairs_to_labels([(0, 1), (1, 2), (4, 5)], n=6)
[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md

# equate.evaluate.metrics

Pairwise and cluster-level match metrics, dependency-light.

Two granularities, kept explicit (research doc 14, §2): [`pairwise_prf()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.pairwise_prf) scores pair
sets; [`bcubed()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.bcubed), [`ceaf()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.ceaf) and [`cluster_metrics()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.cluster_metrics) score a label per record.
**B³ is the default cluster metric** — it alone satisfies all of Amigó’s formal
constraints (§2.4) — with CEAF, ARI and V-measure as complements. ARI and V-measure
delegate to `sklearn.metrics` when it is installed and fall back to the numpy
implementations here otherwise; CEAF’s cluster alignment goes through equate’s own
matcher seam rather than a second Hungarian.

### Functions

| [`bcubed`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.bcubed)(pred_labels, true_labels)                   | B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.                                                                                                           |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ceaf`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.ceaf)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*[, variant, ...]) | CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters.                                                                                           |
| [`cluster_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.cluster_metrics)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*)      | B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness.                                                                                           |
| [`gmd`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.gmd)(pred_labels, true_labels, \*[, ...])           | Generalized merge distance: the cost of the splits and merges that turn the predicted clustering into the true one (Menestrina, Whang & Garcia-Molina, VLDB 2010). |
| [`linear_cost`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.linear_cost)([k1, k2])                              | A cost `k1 + k2 * x * y` — the order-independent family GMD is defined for.                                                                                        |
| [`pair_cost`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.pair_cost)(x, y)                                    | Cost `x * y`: the record pairs a split separates or a merge joins — with it, GMD equals the number of pairwise errors (false positives + false negatives).         |
| [`pairwise_prf`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.pairwise_prf)(pred_pairs, true_pairs, \*[, ...])    | Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.                                                                                            |
| [`unit_cost`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.unit_cost)(x, y)                                    | Cost 1 per split or merge, whatever the sizes (GMD counts operations).                                                                                             |

### equate.evaluate.metrics.bcubed(pred_labels, true_labels)

B³ precision / recall / F1 — the default cluster metric.

Per record: precision is the share of its predicted cluster that truly belongs with
it, recall the share of its true cluster that the prediction kept with it; both are
averaged over records.

```pycon
>>> s = bcubed([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1])
>>> round(s.precision, 3), round(s.recall, 3)
(0.75, 0.667)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.ceaf(pred_labels, true_labels, , variant='entity', matcher='optimal')

CEAF: score the best one-to-one alignment of predicted to true clusters.

`variant='entity'` (CEAF-e, φ4) weighs each aligned pair by
`2|K∩R| / (|K|+|R|)` and normalises by the number of clusters;
`variant='mention'` (CEAF-m, φ3) weighs by `|K∩R|` and normalises by the
number of records. The alignment is a maximum-weight assignment, resolved through
equate’s [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers) registry (`matcher`), never a
private Hungarian.

```pycon
>>> round(ceaf([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1]).f1, 3)
0.733
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.cluster_metrics(pred_labels, true_labels, , backend='auto')

B³ (the headline), CEAF-e, ARI, V-measure, homogeneity and completeness.

`backend='auto'` uses `sklearn.metrics` for ARI / V-measure when sklearn is
installed and the numpy implementations otherwise; `'numpy'` forces the latter,
`'sklearn'` requires the former. The two agree; the choice only exists so the
core install needs neither.

```pycon
>>> m = cluster_metrics([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1], backend='numpy')
>>> sorted(m)
['ari', 'b3_f1', 'b3_precision', 'b3_recall', 'ceaf_e_f1', 'completeness',
 'homogeneity', 'v_measure']
```

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.gmd(pred_labels, true_labels, \*, merge_cost=<function unit_cost>, split_cost=<function unit_cost>)

Generalized merge distance: the cost of the splits and merges that turn the
predicted clustering into the true one (Menestrina, Whang & Garcia-Molina, VLDB 2010).

`split_cost(x, y)` prices splitting a cluster of `x + y` records into `x` and
`y`; `merge_cost(x, y)` merging an `x`- and a `y`-record cluster. The defaults
([`unit_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.unit_cost)) count operations; [`pair_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.pair_cost) for both gives the pairwise
error count; [`linear_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.metrics.html.md#equate.evaluate.metrics.linear_cost) `(k1, k2)` is `k1 + k2·x·y`. Unlike F-measures it
is a distance (`0` = identical), and its costs let an application say whether a
wrong merge hurts more than a missed one. Linear time.

As in the paper, this is the cost of the *legal* path — split each predicted cluster
along the true clusters, then merge the pieces of each true cluster — and the costs
must be **operation-order independent** (constant, `k·x·y`, or `k1 + k2·x·y`):
for other costs the result can depend on the labels’ names. With unit costs a path
that merges first can occasionally be cheaper; GMD is defined as the legal path.

```pycon
>>> gmd([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1])   # split {2, 3}, merge {2} into {0, 1}
2.0
>>> gmd([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0, 1], merge_cost=pair_cost, split_cost=pair_cost)
3.0
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.linear_cost(k1=0.0, k2=1.0)

A cost `k1 + k2 * x * y` — the order-independent family GMD is defined for.

```pycon
>>> linear_cost(1, 0)(3, 4), linear_cost(0, 1)(3, 4)
(1.0, 12.0)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.pair_cost(x, y)

Cost `x * y`: the record pairs a split separates or a merge joins — with it,
GMD equals the number of pairwise errors (false positives + false negatives).

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.pairwise_prf(pred_pairs, true_pairs, , self_join=False)

Pairwise precision / recall / F1 of predicted pairs against gold pairs.

`self_join=True` (deduplication within one collection) treats `(i, j)` and
`(j, i)` as one pair and drops `(i, i)`; otherwise pairs are `(row of A, row
of B)` and orientation matters.

```pycon
>>> s = pairwise_prf([(0, 0), (1, 2)], [(0, 0), (1, 1)])
>>> s.precision, s.recall, s.support
(0.5, 0.5, 2)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

### equate.evaluate.metrics.unit_cost(x, y)

Cost 1 per split or merge, whatever the sizes (GMD counts operations).

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md

# equate.evaluate.ranking

Threshold-free and ranking metrics, and threshold selection as its own step.

[`pr_auc()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.pr_auc) (average precision) summarises a scorer without choosing a threshold and
stays honest under the heavy class imbalance of matching, where ROC-AUC flatters
(research doc 14, §4). [`select_threshold()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.select_threshold) is deliberately separate from scoring:
tuning on the test set should be something a user does on purpose, never by accident
(§3, §7.2).

### Functions

| [`pr_auc`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.pr_auc)(scores, y_true)                           | Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.             |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ranking_metrics`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.ranking_metrics)(ranked, gold, \*[, ks])          | Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.                              |
| [`select_threshold`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.ranking.html.md#equate.evaluate.ranking.select_threshold)(scores, y_true, \*[, optimize]) | The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`. |

### equate.evaluate.ranking.pr_auc(scores, y_true)

Average precision: the area under the precision-recall step curve.

Records with tied scores enter the ranking together (one threshold step), so the
figure does not depend on the input order of ties. No positives → `nan`.

```pycon
>>> round(pr_auc([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.1], [1, 0, 1, 0]), 3)
0.833
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### equate.evaluate.ranking.ranking_metrics(ranked, gold, , ks=(1, 5, 10))

Recall@k, MRR and MAP for ranked candidate lists.

`ranked[q]` is query `q`’s candidates, best first; `gold[q]` is its true match
or a collection of them. Queries with no gold are skipped; a query whose gold never
appears contributes 0.

```pycon
>>> m = ranking_metrics({'a': ['x', 'y'], 'b': ['z', 'w']}, {'a': 'y', 'b': 'z'}, ks=(1,))
>>> m['recall_at_1'], m['mrr']
(0.5, 0.75)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### equate.evaluate.ranking.select_threshold(scores, y_true, , optimize='f1')

The score threshold (`score >= t` predicts a match) that maximises `optimize`.

Pass **validation** scores and labels. `optimize` is `'f1'`, `'precision'` or
`'recall'`; ties go to the higher threshold (fewer predicted matches). Returns the
threshold and the `Scores` it achieves on the data it was chosen on — which
are therefore optimistic, and are not a test result.

```pycon
>>> t, s = select_threshold([0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3], [1, 1, 0, 1])
>>> t, round(s.f1, 3)
(0.3, 0.857)
```

* **Return type:**
  [`tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float), [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)]


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md

# equate.evaluate.scores

The one score type every metric returns: precision and recall, never F1 alone.

[`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores) is the SSOT for how a match quality figure is represented (research
doc 14, §2.5): an F1 without the precision/recall it averages hides whether a matcher
is over- or under-linking, so the type carries all three plus the support they were
computed over.

### Classes

| [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)(precision, recall, f1[, support])   | Precision, recall and their harmonic mean, plus what they were computed over.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.evaluate.scores.Scores(precision, recall, f1, support=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Precision, recall and their harmonic mean, plus what they were computed over.

```pycon
>>> s = Scores.from_counts(tp=3, n_pred=4, n_true=6)
>>> s.precision, s.recall, round(s.f1, 3)
(0.75, 0.5, 0.6)
>>> s.support
6
```

#### as_dict()

The fields as a plain dict (for tables, JSON, a dataframe row).

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

#### *classmethod* from_counts(, tp, n_pred, n_true)

Build from true-positive, predicted and gold counts.

An empty prediction has precision 1.0 (it asserted nothing false); an empty gold
set has recall 1.0 (there was nothing to find). Both empty is a perfect score.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

#### *classmethod* from_pr(precision, recall, , support=None)

Build from precision and recall; F1 is derived, so it can never disagree.

* **Return type:**
  [`Scores`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.scores.html.md#equate.evaluate.scores.Scores)

#### support *: [Optional](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]* *= None*

the size of the gold side (true pairs, or records for a cluster metric)


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md

# equate.evaluate.split

Leakage-aware splitting: split over entities, so test entities are unseen.

The most common way a matching benchmark lies is a pair-level split: the same real-world
entity shows up in train and test, and the model memorises it (research doc 14, §7.2).
[`entity_split()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.entity_split) makes the right split the easy one — it partitions **entity ids**,
so every record of an entity lands in exactly one part — and [`assert_no_leakage()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.assert_no_leakage)
is the cheap post-hoc guard for a split made some other way.

### Functions

| [`assert_no_leakage`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.assert_no_leakage)(entity_ids, \*parts)       | Raise `AssertionError` if any entity has records in more than one of `parts`.   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`entity_split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.entity_split)(entity_ids, \*[, ratios, seed]) | Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.       |

### Classes

| [`Split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.Split)(train, val, test)   | Record indices of each part; the entity ids of a part never occur in another.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.evaluate.split.Split(train, val, test)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Record indices of each part; the entity ids of a part never occur in another.

### equate.evaluate.split.assert_no_leakage(entity_ids, \*parts)

Raise `AssertionError` if any entity has records in more than one of `parts`.

```pycon
>>> assert_no_leakage([0, 0, 1], [0], [1])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
AssertionError: entity 0 appears in parts 0 and 1 — the split leaks it
```

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### equate.evaluate.split.entity_split(entity_ids, , ratios=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), seed=0)

Split records into train / val / test by entity, never by record or pair.

`entity_ids[i]` is record `i`’s true entity (e.g. from
[`cross_pairs_to_labels()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#equate.evaluate.cross_pairs_to_labels) over a two-table gold matching).
Entities, not records, are shuffled (`seed`) and cut by `ratios`, so the parts
are disjoint in entities and roughly — not exactly — proportional in records.

```pycon
>>> s = entity_split([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], seed=1)
>>> assert_no_leakage([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6], s.train, s.test)
>>> sorted(s.train + s.val + s.test) == list(range(10))
True
```

* **Return type:**
  [`Split`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.split.html.md#equate.evaluate.split.Split)


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md

# equate.evaluate.store

Where downloaded benchmark data lives: a store (a `MutableMapping`), never the package.

Benchmark loaders read their raw files through [`fetch()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.fetch), which takes the bytes from a
*store* when they are there and otherwise downloads them once, checks them against a
pinned SHA-256, and writes them to the store. The store is any `MutableMapping[str,
bytes]` — a `dict` in tests, a `dol` store for S3 or a database — and defaults to
[`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.FileStore) over [`data_dir()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.data_dir) (`$EQUATE_DATA_DIR`, else
`$XDG_DATA_HOME/equate/benchmarks`, else `~/.local/share/equate/benchmarks`).

Downloads need nothing beyond the standard library; the `equate[benchmarks]` extra is
declared so that `pip install 'equate[benchmarks]'` stays the stable spelling as
loaders gain optional dependencies.

### Functions

| [`data_dir`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.data_dir)()                                     | The default root of the benchmark cache (not created until something is written).                                                                           |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`default_store`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.default_store)()                                | The default benchmark cache: a [`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.FileStore) over [`data_dir()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.data_dir). |
| [`fetch`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.fetch)(key, source, \*[, store, download, get]) | The bytes of `source`, from `store` if cached, else downloaded and cached.                                                                                  |
| [`http_get`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.http_get)(url, \*[, timeout])                   | Download `url` (stdlib `urllib`) and return its bytes.                                                                                                      |

### Classes

| [`Source`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.Source)(url[, sha256])   | A remote file: where it is, and the SHA-256 its bytes must have.        |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.FileStore)(root)         | A `MutableMapping[str, bytes]` over the files under `root` (dol-style). |

### *class* equate.evaluate.store.FileStore(root)

Bases: [`MutableMapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.MutableMapping)

A `MutableMapping[str, bytes]` over the files under `root` (dol-style).

Keys are relative POSIX paths (`'wdc_products/80multi.zip'`) of plain names: no
`..`/`.`/empty segment, backslash, drive or `.part` suffix, so a key cannot escape
`root` on any platform. Writes are atomic even with concurrent writers (a unique
temporary file in the same directory, then a rename), so a reader never sees a
truncated file.

```pycon
>>> import tempfile
>>> s = FileStore(tempfile.mkdtemp())
>>> s['suite/file.csv'] = b'a,b'
>>> list(s), s['suite/file.csv']
(['suite/file.csv'], b'a,b')
```

### *class* equate.evaluate.store.Source(url, sha256=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A remote file: where it is, and the SHA-256 its bytes must have.

`sha256=None` skips the integrity check (for a file whose publisher re-issues it).

### equate.evaluate.store.data_dir()

The default root of the benchmark cache (not created until something is written).

* **Return type:**
  [`Path`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.Path)

### equate.evaluate.store.default_store()

The default benchmark cache: a [`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.FileStore) over [`data_dir()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.data_dir).

* **Return type:**
  [`FileStore`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.FileStore)

### equate.evaluate.store.fetch(key, source, , store=None, download=True, get=None)

The bytes of `source`, from `store` if cached, else downloaded and cached.

The bytes are checked against `source.sha256` **every time**, cached or not: a
cached copy that no longer matches (corrupted on disk, or a pin updated for a
re-issued file) is downloaded again; a download that does not match raises
`ValueError` and nothing is written. With `download=False` a missing or stale
key raises `FileNotFoundError` instead of reaching the network. `get(url) ->
bytes` is the downloader (default [`http_get()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.http_get)).

* **Return type:**
  [`bytes`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#bytes)

### equate.evaluate.store.http_get(url, , timeout=120)

Download `url` (stdlib `urllib`) and return its bytes.

* **Return type:**
  [`bytes`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#bytes)


# _autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md

# equate.evaluate.suites

Loaders for the standard matching benchmarks, fetched on first use into a store.

Registered in `benchmarks` (research doc 14, §6 and §8.3):

- `abt_buy`, `amazon_google`, `dblp_acm` — the product and bibliographic tables the
  Magellan / DeepMatcher suite made standard. `source='leipzig'` (default) loads the
  original tables of the Leipzig database group with their **complete** gold mapping
  (CC BY 4.0). `source='deepmatcher'` (named `<suite>_deepmatcher`, so a report keeps
  the two apart) loads DeepMatcher’s preprocessed tables with its
  canonical labelled train/valid/test pairs in `Benchmark.pairs`; its gold is the
  labelled positives only, which misses true matches its blocking dropped (`meta`
  says how many), so it is the source for comparing pair classifiers with published
  numbers, not for scoring whole-table matching.
- `wdc_products` — WDC Products (Peeters, Der & Bizer 2024), the difficulty-controlled
  product benchmark: `corner_cases` (80/50/20 %), `unseen` (0/50/100 % of test
  entities absent from training) and `dev_size` (small/medium/large). Built from its
  multi-class files, with its train/valid/test sets as `Benchmark.splits`.

Every loader takes `store=` (any `MutableMapping`; default
[`default_store()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.store.html.md#equate.evaluate.store.default_store)), `download=`, `get=` (the downloader)
and `verify=` (check the pinned SHA-256, on every read — default on; off only for a
trusted mirror), puts the publisher’s record ids in `Benchmark.ids`, and fills `meta` with
`source`, `license`, a `difficulty` sentence and a measured `difficulty_profile`
([`difficulty_profile()`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.difficulty.html.md#equate.evaluate.difficulty.difficulty_profile), cached in the store).

### Module Attributes

| [`MAGELLAN_SOURCES`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md#equate.evaluate.suites.MAGELLAN_SOURCES)   | the selectable sources of the three Magellan/DeepMatcher tables   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`abt_buy`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md#equate.evaluate.suites.abt_buy)(\*\*config)                           | Abt-Buy: 1081 × 1092 product offers, 1097 matches (Leipzig; textual, hard).      |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`amazon_google`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md#equate.evaluate.suites.amazon_google)(\*\*config)                     | Amazon-Google: 1363 × 3226 software products, 1300 matches (Leipzig; hard).      |
| [`dblp_acm`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md#equate.evaluate.suites.dblp_acm)(\*\*config)                          | DBLP-ACM: 2616 × 2294 publications, 2224 matches (Leipzig; easy).                |
| [`wdc_products`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.suites.html.md#equate.evaluate.suites.wdc_products)(\*[, corner_cases, unseen, ...]) | WDC Products as a two-table benchmark with its canonical train/valid/test split. |

### equate.evaluate.suites.MAGELLAN_SOURCES *= ('leipzig', 'deepmatcher')*

the selectable sources of the three Magellan/DeepMatcher tables

### equate.evaluate.suites.abt_buy(\*\*config)

Abt-Buy: 1081 × 1092 product offers, 1097 matches (Leipzig; textual, hard).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### equate.evaluate.suites.amazon_google(\*\*config)

Amazon-Google: 1363 × 3226 software products, 1300 matches (Leipzig; hard).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### equate.evaluate.suites.dblp_acm(\*\*config)

DBLP-ACM: 2616 × 2294 publications, 2224 matches (Leipzig; easy).

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)

### equate.evaluate.suites.wdc_products(, corner_cases=80, unseen=100, dev_size='large', seed=0, store=None, download=True, get=None, verify=True, profile=True)

WDC Products as a two-table benchmark with its canonical train/valid/test split.

The defaults pick the hardest generalization variant — 80 % corner cases, every test
entity unseen in training (research doc 14, §7.6) — with the large development set.
Gold pairs every `a`/`b` offer of the same product, across parts too (a seen test
product matches its training offers); only the test-part gold is scored. Row order
within each part is shuffled with `seed`. `meta['leakage']` counts test offers
that also appear, identically, in train or valid. WDC’s own files have such overlap:
hundreds in the 50 %-unseen variants, a few in valid for 0 %. A warning says so.

* **Return type:**
  [`Benchmark`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.benchmark.html.md#equate.evaluate.benchmark.Benchmark)


# _autosummary/equate.facade.html.md

# equate.facade

The equate facade: the one-line `match(A, B)` entry point.

Wires the pipeline — featurize → compare (over the blocker’s candidates) → match — with
sensible defaults, and returns a structured [`equate.base.Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching). Every stage is
swappable by one keyword (decision register D4): `featurize=`, `compare=`, `block=`,
`how=`. This is the canonical case (doc 10 §1): two collections -> optimally-matched
(and scored) pairs, zero config.

### Functions

| [`match`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.match)(A[, B, featurize, compare, block, ...])     | Match two collections into a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of scored `(i, j)` pairs.                                  |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`score_matrix`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.score_matrix)(A, B, \*[, featurize, compare, ...]) | Score `A` against `B` into a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) — stages ① and ②.                                    |
| [`dedupe`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe)(A, \*[, compare, block, threshold, ...])   | Deduplicate a single collection into entity groups.                                                                                                                    |
| [`resolve`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.resolve)(\*collections, \*\*kwargs)                | Resolve entities across multiple collections: pool them (in order) and [`dedupe()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe) -> a Partition over the pooled items. |

### equate.facade.dedupe(A, , compare='ratio', block=None, threshold=0.7, cluster='connected_components', sense=None)

Deduplicate a single collection into entity groups.

Self-compares `A`’s candidate pairs, keeps those passing `threshold`, and clusters
them -> a [`Partition`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Partition) over `A` (iterate it for the duplicate
`(i, j)` pairs; `.groups()` for the clusters). `block` (a blocker) restricts the
candidate pairs (self-join); the default compares all `i < j` pairs. `cluster` is
`'connected_components'` (transitive closure) or `'correlation'`. `sense` defaults
to the comparator’s declared polarity — a *distance* comparator (e.g.
`levenshtein_distance`) uses `'minimize'` so *lower* scores link, a similarity uses
`'maximize'`.

```pycon
>>> from equate import dedupe
>>> dedupe(['Jon Smith', 'Jon Smyth', 'Kate Doe'], threshold=0.8).groups()
{0: [0, 1], 1: [2]}
```

### equate.facade.match(A, B=None, , featurize=None, compare=None, block=None, how='assign', threshold=None, cluster='connected_components', sense=None)

Match two collections into a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of scored `(i, j)` pairs.

Pipeline (each stage swappable by one keyword):

- **featurize / compare** — with `compare=None` (default), the *vector route*:
  featurize both sides with `featurize` (TF-IDF by default) and score by cosine.
  With a `compare` comparator (a registered name or a callable), the \*direct
  pairwise route\* on the raw items.
- **block** — `None` (default) scores all pairs (dense); a blocker (name/callable)
  scores only the candidate pairs into a sparse matrix, and the matcher stays sparse-aware.
- **sense** — `None` (default) reads it off the comparator’s declared polarity: a
  *distance* comparator (`'dtw'`, `'levenshtein_distance'`) is minimized, anything
  else maximized. Pass `'maximize'` / `'minimize'` to override.
- **how** — the matcher objective: `'assign'` (optimal 1:1, the default),
  `'greedy'`, `'stable'`, or `'soft'` (an optimal-transport plan; `.plan` is set).

Returns a `Matching`: iterate it for `(i, j)` pairs, `dict(...)` it for a mapping,
`.labeled_pairs()` for `(A[i], B[j])`; `.scores` holds each matched pair’s score.

```pycon
>>> keys = ['apple pie', 'banana split', 'cherry tart']
>>> values = ['cherry tarte', 'aple pie', 'banana split']
>>> m = match(keys, values, compare='ratio')
>>> dict(m.labeled_pairs())
{'apple pie': 'aple pie', 'banana split': 'banana split', 'cherry tart': 'cherry tarte'}
```

### equate.facade.resolve(\*collections, \*\*kwargs)

Resolve entities across multiple collections: pool them (in order) and
[`dedupe()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe) -> a Partition over the pooled items. Generalizes cross-collection
matching to n-way linkage. Accepts the same keywords as [`dedupe()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.dedupe).

### equate.facade.score_matrix(A, B, , featurize=None, compare=None, block=None, sense=None)

Score `A` against `B` into a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) — stages ① and ②.

The scoring half of [`match()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.match), exposed on its own for callers that keep the scores
and match later or repeatedly (the interactive loop re-solves from them on every edit;
see [`equate.service`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#module-equate.service)). The keywords mean exactly what they mean in [`match()`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#equate.facade.match):
the default is the TF-IDF + cosine vector route; `compare=` takes the direct pairwise
route; `block=` scores only the blocker’s candidates into a sparse matrix; `sense`
defaults to the comparator’s declared polarity.

```pycon
>>> sm = score_matrix(['apple', 'kiwi'], ['kiwis', 'apples'], compare='ratio')
>>> sm.shape, sm.sense
((2, 2), 'maximize')
```


# _autosummary/equate.featurize.columns.html.md

# equate.featurize.columns

Column featurizers: a column (a sequence of cell values) as a comparable object.

Lifting the pipeline from cells to columns (research doc 07, §8.1): a column’s values are
its signal when headers are missing or untrustworthy. [`value_set()`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.columns.html.md#equate.featurize.columns.value_set) represents each
column as the set of its distinct, normalized, non-missing values — the input of the set
comparators (`jaccard`, `overlap`, `containment`) used for join-key discovery and
near-duplicate columns.

### Functions

| [`value_set`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.columns.html.md#equate.featurize.columns.value_set)(columns, \*[, normalize])   | Each column as the `frozenset` of its normalized, non-missing values (batched).                                                                     |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`normalize_value`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.columns.html.md#equate.featurize.columns.normalize_value)(v)                    | The default cell normalization: text, stripped and lower-cased; `1.0` and `1` read alike (an integral real drops its `.0`, numpy scalars included). |
| [`is_missing`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.columns.html.md#equate.featurize.columns.is_missing)(v)                         | `None`, an empty/blank string, a NaN of any float type, or pandas' `NA` / `NaT`.                                                                    |

### equate.featurize.columns.is_missing(v)

`None`, an empty/blank string, a NaN of any float type, or pandas’ `NA` / `NaT`.

```pycon
>>> [is_missing(v) for v in (None, ' ', float('nan'), 0, 'x')]
[True, True, True, False, False]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)

### equate.featurize.columns.normalize_value(v)

The default cell normalization: text, stripped and lower-cased; `1.0` and `1`
read alike (an integral real drops its `.0`, numpy scalars included).

```pycon
>>> normalize_value('  Paris '), normalize_value(3.0), normalize_value(3)
('paris', '3', '3')
```

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### equate.featurize.columns.value_set(columns, \*, normalize=<function normalize_value>)

Each column as the `frozenset` of its normalized, non-missing values (batched).

```pycon
>>> [sorted(s) for s in value_set([['Paris', 'paris ', None], [1, 2.0]])]
[['paris'], ['1', '2']]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)


# _autosummary/equate.featurize.graph.html.md

# equate.featurize.graph

Graph featurizers (stage ①): turn whole graphs into vectors (graph kernels).

A graph kernel maps each graph to a feature vector, so matching a collection of graphs
goes back to the *indexable* featurize-then-compare route: cosine scoring, ANN/LSH
blocking, the flat matchers — with no special-casing in the match layer (doc `12` §3.4,
decision D8).

- [`WLFeaturizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.graph.html.md#equate.featurize.graph.WLFeaturizer) (`'wl'`, core) — the **Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree** feature map
  (Shervashidze et al. 2011): relabel each node by its own label plus the multiset of
  its neighbors’ labels, `iterations` times, and count the labels seen. Linear in the
  number of edges per iteration; pure numpy/scipy.
- [`grakel_featurizer()`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.graph.html.md#equate.featurize.graph.grakel_featurizer) (`'grakel'`, `equate[graph-kernels]`) — any GraKeL
  kernel (WL, shortest-path, graphlet, …) as an *empirical kernel map*: a graph’s
  vector is its kernel value against each corpus graph.

Graphs may be networkx graphs, `{node: neighbors}` mappings or adjacency matrices
(see `equate._graph.as_graph()`).

### Module Attributes

| [`DFLT_WL_ITERATIONS`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.graph.html.md#equate.featurize.graph.DFLT_WL_ITERATIONS)   | WL refinement rounds (the subtree depth).   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`grakel_featurizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.graph.html.md#equate.featurize.graph.grakel_featurizer)(\*[, kernel, label])   | A GraKeL graph kernel as a fittable featurizer — requires `equate[graph-kernels]`.   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Classes

| [`WLFeaturizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.graph.html.md#equate.featurize.graph.WLFeaturizer)(\*[, iterations, label])   | Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree featurizer: `graphs -> L2-normalized sparse counts`.   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### equate.featurize.graph.DFLT_WL_ITERATIONS *= 3*

WL refinement rounds (the subtree depth). 3-5 is the usual range.

### *class* equate.featurize.graph.WLFeaturizer(, iterations=3, label=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree featurizer: `graphs -> L2-normalized sparse counts`.

Fit on a corpus of graphs to fix the vocabulary of WL labels (one column per label
seen in any round), then transform graphs into count vectors over it; labels never
seen in the corpus are ignored. A fitted instance is itself a batch featurizer.

Two isomorphic graphs (same labels) always get the same vector; the converse holds
up to the WL test’s power (it cannot tell some regular graphs apart). Neighbors are
*out*-neighbors (a directed graph is refined along its edges), and edge weights are
ignored – the subtree kernel counts structure, not strength.

```pycon
>>> path3 = {0: [1], 1: [0, 2], 2: [1]}
>>> triangle = {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 2], 2: [0, 1]}
>>> wl = WLFeaturizer(iterations=2).fit([path3, triangle])
>>> X = wl([path3, {'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a', 'c'], 'c': ['b']}, triangle])
>>> cos = (X @ X.T).toarray()  # rows are L2-normalized
>>> float(round(cos[0, 1], 6)), bool(cos[0, 2] < 1)  # isomorphic -> 1; path vs triangle < 1
(1.0, True)
```

#### fit(graphs)

Learn the WL-label vocabulary from `graphs`; returns `self`.

#### transform(graphs)

Count vectors (`csr`, one row per graph), L2-normalized.

### equate.featurize.graph.grakel_featurizer(, kernel='WeisfeilerLehman', label=None, \*\*kernel_params)

A GraKeL graph kernel as a fittable featurizer — requires `equate[graph-kernels]`.

`kernel` names a class in `grakel.kernels` (`'WeisfeilerLehman'`,
`'ShortestPath'`, `'GraphletSampling'`, …), built with `normalize=True` and
`**kernel_params`. After `fit(corpus)`, a graph’s vector is its (normalized)
kernel value against each corpus graph — the empirical kernel map, so cosine/ANN work
on it like on any embedding.


# _autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md

# equate.featurize

The featurize stage (①): map objects to comparable representations.

A *featurizer* is a batch callable `Iterable[object] -> representations`. The default
is a pure numpy/scipy char-n-gram TF-IDF ([`equate.featurize.tfidf`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md#module-equate.featurize.tfidf)) — no heavy
dependencies; dense embedders (SBERT, OpenAI, …) are optional extras
([`equate.featurize.text`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md#module-equate.featurize.text)). Select a featurizer by name via the [`featurizers`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.featurizers)
registry, or pass a callable. Corpus-dependent featurizers (TF-IDF) are built by
fitting on a corpus, which [`resolve_featurizer()`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.resolve_featurizer) handles.

### Module Attributes

| [`featurizers`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.featurizers)   | the featurize-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`identity`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.identity)(objects)                                 | The identity featurizer: use the objects themselves as their representation.                                                                                                                      |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`record_text`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.record_text)(obj)                                  | Text of `obj`: a mapping's non-empty values joined by spaces, else `str(obj)`.                                                                                                                    |
| [`value_set`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.value_set)(columns, \*[, normalize])               | Each column as the `frozenset` of its normalized, non-missing values (batched).                                                                                                                   |
| [`resolve_featurizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.resolve_featurizer)([spec, corpus])                | Resolve `spec` to a ready-to-use batch featurizer.                                                                                                                                                |
| [`mk_tfidf`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.mk_tfidf)(\*learn_texts[, ngram_range, lowercase]) | Fit a char-n-gram TF-IDF on the given collection(s) and return the fitted, callable batch featurizer — the pure numpy/scipy replacement for the legacy grub-backed `equate.util.mk_text_to_vect`. |
| [`char_ngrams`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.char_ngrams)(text[, ngram_range, lowercase])       | Character n-grams of `text` over the inclusive `ngram_range`.                                                                                                                                     |
| [`grakel_featurizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.grakel_featurizer)(\*[, kernel, label])            | A GraKeL graph kernel as a fittable featurizer — requires `equate[graph-kernels]`.                                                                                                                |

### Classes

| [`TfidfFeaturizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.TfidfFeaturizer)(\*[, ngram_range, lowercase])   | Fittable char-n-gram TF-IDF featurizer producing L2-normalized sparse vectors.                                                                                                                                                                  |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`FeaturizerMeta`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.FeaturizerMeta)([output_kinds, normalize, ...])  | Declared properties of a featurizer (decision register D9), so the framework can pick a legal index/metric, auto-apply a required query/passage prefix, refuse a non-commercial model in a commercial context, and offer Matryoshka truncation. |
| [`WLFeaturizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#equate.featurize.WLFeaturizer)(\*[, iterations, label])           | Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree featurizer: `graphs -> L2-normalized sparse counts`.                                                                                                                                                                  |

### *class* equate.featurize.FeaturizerMeta(output_kinds=('vector',), normalize=False, dim=None, license=None, max_seq_len=None, query_prefix=None, passage_prefix=None, truncatable_to=())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Declared properties of a featurizer (decision register D9), so the framework
can pick a legal index/metric, auto-apply a required query/passage prefix, refuse a
non-commercial model in a commercial context, and offer Matryoshka truncation.

- `output_kinds`: what the representation is — `'vector'` / `'set'` /
  `'bitstring'` / `'scalar'` / `'structured'` (a multi-functional embedder may
  emit several, e.g. dense + sparse);
- `normalize`: whether output vectors are already L2-normalized;
- `dim` / `max_seq_len`: dimensionality and max input length, when fixed;
- `license`: SPDX/label, so a commercial context can refuse non-commercial models;
- `query_prefix` / `passage_prefix`: instruction prefixes some embedders require
  (e.g. E5’s `"query: "` / `"passage: "`) — a silent-omission footgun;
- `truncatable_to`: Matryoshka dims the embedding can be safely truncated to.

### *class* equate.featurize.TfidfFeaturizer(, ngram_range=(2, 4), lowercase=True)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Fittable char-n-gram TF-IDF featurizer producing L2-normalized sparse vectors.

Fit on a corpus to learn the vocabulary and inverse document frequencies, then
transform texts to vectors. A fitted instance is itself a batch featurizer, so
`vecs = featurizer(texts)` works.

#### meta *= FeaturizerMeta(output_kinds=('vector',), normalize=True, dim=None, license='core', max_seq_len=None, query_prefix=None, passage_prefix=None, truncatable_to=())*

declared metadata (see equate.base.FeaturizerMeta)

### *class* equate.featurize.WLFeaturizer(, iterations=3, label=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree featurizer: `graphs -> L2-normalized sparse counts`.

Fit on a corpus of graphs to fix the vocabulary of WL labels (one column per label
seen in any round), then transform graphs into count vectors over it; labels never
seen in the corpus are ignored. A fitted instance is itself a batch featurizer.

Two isomorphic graphs (same labels) always get the same vector; the converse holds
up to the WL test’s power (it cannot tell some regular graphs apart). Neighbors are
*out*-neighbors (a directed graph is refined along its edges), and edge weights are
ignored – the subtree kernel counts structure, not strength.

```pycon
>>> path3 = {0: [1], 1: [0, 2], 2: [1]}
>>> triangle = {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 2], 2: [0, 1]}
>>> wl = WLFeaturizer(iterations=2).fit([path3, triangle])
>>> X = wl([path3, {'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a', 'c'], 'c': ['b']}, triangle])
>>> cos = (X @ X.T).toarray()  # rows are L2-normalized
>>> float(round(cos[0, 1], 6)), bool(cos[0, 2] < 1)  # isomorphic -> 1; path vs triangle < 1
(1.0, True)
```

#### fit(graphs)

Learn the WL-label vocabulary from `graphs`; returns `self`.

#### transform(graphs)

Count vectors (`csr`, one row per graph), L2-normalized.

### equate.featurize.char_ngrams(text, ngram_range=(2, 4), , lowercase=True)

Character n-grams of `text` over the inclusive `ngram_range`.

The whole string is padded with one leading and one trailing space (so prefixes and
suffixes are captured), and n-grams slide over the entire padded string — they \*may
therefore span the spaces between words\*. This is deliberate (it helps fuzzy
name/SKU matching) and differs from scikit-learn’s per-word `char_wb` analyzer. A
text too short for any `n` in the range falls back to the padded string itself, so
tiny or empty inputs still yield a (single) feature rather than an all-zero vector.
A record (a mapping) is read through [`record_text()`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.records.html.md#equate.featurize.records.record_text);
any other non-string raises `TypeError`.

```pycon
>>> char_ngrams('cat', (2, 3))
[' c', 'ca', 'at', 't ', ' ca', 'cat', 'at ']
>>> char_ngrams('', (3, 4))          # too short for any n: falls back to the padding
['  ']
```

### equate.featurize.featurizers *= <equate.registry.Registry object>*

the featurize-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)

### equate.featurize.grakel_featurizer(, kernel='WeisfeilerLehman', label=None, \*\*kernel_params)

A GraKeL graph kernel as a fittable featurizer — requires `equate[graph-kernels]`.

`kernel` names a class in `grakel.kernels` (`'WeisfeilerLehman'`,
`'ShortestPath'`, `'GraphletSampling'`, …), built with `normalize=True` and
`**kernel_params`. After `fit(corpus)`, a graph’s vector is its (normalized)
kernel value against each corpus graph — the empirical kernel map, so cosine/ANN work
on it like on any embedding.

### equate.featurize.identity(objects)

The identity featurizer: use the objects themselves as their representation.

This is the degenerate case that recovers exact matching (φ = id).

### equate.featurize.mk_tfidf(\*learn_texts, ngram_range=(2, 4), lowercase=True)

Fit a char-n-gram TF-IDF on the given collection(s) and return the fitted,
callable batch featurizer — the pure numpy/scipy replacement for the legacy
grub-backed `equate.util.mk_text_to_vect`.

### equate.featurize.record_text(obj)

Text of `obj`: a mapping’s non-empty values joined by spaces, else `str(obj)`.

```pycon
>>> record_text({'name': 'Jon Smith', 'city': 'Paris', 'zip': None})
'Jon Smith Paris'
>>> record_text(42)
'42'
```

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### equate.featurize.resolve_featurizer(spec=None, , corpus=None, \*\*config)

Resolve `spec` to a ready-to-use batch featurizer.

- `None` -> the default `'tfidf'`;
- a registered name (`str`) -> built via its factory (`**config` is forwarded, so
  an unknown option raises rather than being silently ignored);
- a callable -> returned as-is (assumed already a batch featurizer).

A *fittable* featurizer (one exposing `fit`, e.g. TF-IDF) is fit on `corpus`
here — and a corpus is then required: resolving a fittable featurizer without one
raises immediately (a clear error at the call site) instead of returning a
half-built object that only fails later inside `transform`.

### equate.featurize.value_set(columns, \*, normalize=<function normalize_value>)

Each column as the `frozenset` of its normalized, non-missing values (batched).

```pycon
>>> [sorted(s) for s in value_set([['Paris', 'paris ', None], [1, 2.0]])]
[['paris'], ['1', '2']]
```

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)

# _autosummary/equate.featurize.records.html.md

# equate.featurize.records

The text of an object, for text featurizers: a record (mapping) is its joined values.

Text featurizers (TF-IDF, embedders) need a string. A record — a dict from JSON, a CSV row
— has none of its own, so it is read as its non-empty values joined by spaces; anything
else as `str(obj)`. This is what lets `match(records_a, records_b)` work on the
default vector route.

### Functions

| [`record_text`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.records.html.md#equate.featurize.records.record_text)(obj)   | Text of `obj`: a mapping's non-empty values joined by spaces, else `str(obj)`.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### equate.featurize.records.record_text(obj)

Text of `obj`: a mapping’s non-empty values joined by spaces, else `str(obj)`.

```pycon
>>> record_text({'name': 'Jon Smith', 'city': 'Paris', 'zip': None})
'Jon Smith Paris'
>>> record_text(42)
'42'
```

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)


# _autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md

# equate.featurize.text

Dense text-embedding featurizers, behind optional extras.

Each is a *lazily-built* strategy: the heavy library is imported only when the
strategy is actually constructed, via `equate._dependencies.require()`, so a
missing extra raises a friendly `MissingDependencyError` instead of breaking
`import equate`. A representative set is provided here; more embedders (bge-m3, e5,
nomic, cohere, voyage, and image/audio modalities) are added the same way as their
stages land — see the `equate-dev-add-strategy` skill.

### Functions

| [`sbert_featurizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md#equate.featurize.text.sbert_featurizer)(\*[, model])   | Sentence-Transformers (SBERT) embedder — requires `equate[embeddings]`.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`openai_featurizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.text.html.md#equate.featurize.text.openai_featurizer)(\*[, model])  | OpenAI embeddings — requires `equate[api]` and an `OPENAI_API_KEY`.       |

### equate.featurize.text.openai_featurizer(, model='text-embedding-3-small')

OpenAI embeddings — requires `equate[api]` and an `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

Returns a batch featurizer `texts -> embedding matrix`.

### equate.featurize.text.sbert_featurizer(, model='sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
