# _autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md

# equate.featurize.tfidf

Pure-numpy/scipy character-n-gram TF-IDF — equate’s zero-heavy-dependency default
text featurizer (decision register D9). No scikit-learn or grub required.

Character n-grams make it robust to typos and morphology, which suits fuzzy name/SKU
matching; the output vectors are L2-normalized, so cosine similarity is a dot product.

### Functions

| [`mk_tfidf`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md#equate.featurize.tfidf.mk_tfidf)(\*learn_texts[, ngram_range, lowercase])   | Fit a char-n-gram TF-IDF on the given collection(s) and return the fitted, callable batch featurizer — the pure numpy/scipy replacement for the legacy grub-backed `equate.util.mk_text_to_vect`.   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`char_ngrams`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md#equate.featurize.tfidf.char_ngrams)(text[, ngram_range, lowercase])         | Character n-grams of `text` over the inclusive `ngram_range`.                                                                                                                                       |

### Classes

| [`TfidfFeaturizer`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.tfidf.html.md#equate.featurize.tfidf.TfidfFeaturizer)(\*[, ngram_range, lowercase])   | Fittable char-n-gram TF-IDF featurizer producing L2-normalized sparse vectors.   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.featurize.tfidf.TfidfFeaturizer(, ngram_range=(2, 4), lowercase=True)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Fittable char-n-gram TF-IDF featurizer producing L2-normalized sparse vectors.

Fit on a corpus to learn the vocabulary and inverse document frequencies, then
transform texts to vectors. A fitted instance is itself a batch featurizer, so
`vecs = featurizer(texts)` works.

#### meta *= FeaturizerMeta(output_kinds=('vector',), normalize=True, dim=None, license='core', max_seq_len=None, query_prefix=None, passage_prefix=None, truncatable_to=())*

declared metadata (see equate.base.FeaturizerMeta)

### equate.featurize.tfidf.char_ngrams(text, ngram_range=(2, 4), , lowercase=True)

Character n-grams of `text` over the inclusive `ngram_range`.

The whole string is padded with one leading and one trailing space (so prefixes and
suffixes are captured), and n-grams slide over the entire padded string — they \*may
therefore span the spaces between words\*. This is deliberate (it helps fuzzy
name/SKU matching) and differs from scikit-learn’s per-word `char_wb` analyzer. A
text too short for any `n` in the range falls back to the padded string itself, so
tiny or empty inputs still yield a (single) feature rather than an all-zero vector.
A record (a mapping) is read through [`record_text()`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.records.html.md#equate.featurize.records.record_text);
any other non-string raises `TypeError`.

```pycon
>>> char_ngrams('cat', (2, 3))
[' c', 'ca', 'at', 't ', ' ca', 'cat', 'at ']
>>> char_ngrams('', (3, 4))          # too short for any n: falls back to the padding
['  ']
```

### equate.featurize.tfidf.mk_tfidf(\*learn_texts, ngram_range=(2, 4), lowercase=True)

Fit a char-n-gram TF-IDF on the given collection(s) and return the fitted,
callable batch featurizer — the pure numpy/scipy replacement for the legacy
grub-backed `equate.util.mk_text_to_vect`.


# _autosummary/equate.html.md

# equate

Tools for matching things: featurize, compare, and match collections of objects.

Matching is fuzzy correspondence, not exact equality (`==` is the degenerate case).
The public surface is being redesigned around the `featurize -> compare -> match`
decomposition; see `docs/research/` and the `equate-dev-architecture` skill. The
foundation contracts live in [`equate.base`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#module-equate.base).

### Modules

| [`base`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#module-equate.base)               | Foundational contracts and data structures for equate.                                     |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`block`](_autosummary/equate.block.html.md#module-equate.block)             | The block stage (② scalability): candidate generation.                                     |
| [`cluster`](_autosummary/equate.cluster.html.md#module-equate.cluster)         | The resolve/cluster stage (③ grouping): turn pairwise matches into entity groups.          |
| [`compare`](_autosummary/equate.compare.html.md#module-equate.compare)         | The compare stage (②): score how alike two (featurized) items are.                         |
| [`completion`](_autosummary/equate.completion.html.md#module-equate.completion)   | Tabular completion: find join keys, near-duplicate columns, and fill a table from another. |
| [`evaluate`](_autosummary/equate.evaluate.html.md#module-equate.evaluate)       | Evaluate matchers honestly: metrics, leakage-aware splits, and a benchmark harness.        |
| [`facade`](_autosummary/equate.facade.html.md#module-equate.facade)           | The equate facade: the one-line `match(A, B)` entry point.                                 |
| [`featurize`](_autosummary/equate.featurize.html.md#module-equate.featurize)     | The featurize stage (①): map objects to comparable representations.                        |
| [`interactive`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#module-equate.interactive) | The interactive stage: human-in-the-loop review and re-optimization.                       |
| [`matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#module-equate.matching)       | The match stage (③): turn a score matrix into a correspondence.                            |
| [`registry`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#module-equate.registry)       | A tiny name-keyed strategy registry with lazy factories (open-closed dispatch).            |
| [`service`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#module-equate.service)         | The service layer: equate's matching core as JSON-in/JSON-out operations.                  |
| [`util`](_autosummary/equate.util.html.md#module-equate.util)               | Utils for equate.                                                                          |


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.candidate_store.html.md

# equate.interactive.candidate_store

The CandidateStore: per left-item top-k candidates with scores — the SSOT for review
and interactive re-optimization.

Retaining the top-k candidates (not just the single best) is what lets a user edit a match
and have the system re-solve from the remembered alternatives (doc 08-interactive). It is a
plain dataclass so it serializes (e.g. persist with `dol.cache_this` to resume a session).

### Classes

| [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.candidate_store.html.md#equate.interactive.candidate_store.CandidateStore)(candidates[, sense, ...])   | Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.interactive.candidate_store.CandidateStore(candidates, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.

Iterating yields the top-1 `(i, j)` pairs, so `dict(store)` gives the greedy 1:n
match. `row_labels` / `col_labels` name the two collections.

#### *classmethod* from_scores(scores, , k=5, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Build a store of each row’s top-`k` candidates from a (dense or sparse) score
matrix.

A **sparse** matrix considers only its stored (candidate) cells — which is exactly
the blocking semantics (an absent cell is not a candidate), so for a blocked matrix
this intentionally differs from the dense all-cells behavior regardless of `sense`.

#### margin(i)

Confidence gap between item `i`’s top-1 and top-2 candidate scores.

A *small* margin means the top choice is uncertain (two close candidates) — the
signal for review triage and active-learning query selection. An item with 0 or 1
candidates is unambiguous (no rival to be confused with), so its margin is `+inf`
— it sorts LAST in a most-uncertain-first queue, never spuriously to the front.

#### top(i, n=1)

The top-`n` `(right_index, score)` candidates for left item `i`.


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md

# equate.interactive.constraints

Interactive constraints and re-optimization: every user edit is a constraint, not a
recompute.

A *confirm* forces an edge into the assignment; a *reject* forbids one. [`reoptimize()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md#equate.interactive.constraints.reoptimize)
re-solves the optimal assignment honoring the accumulated constraints — the primitive
behind “edit a match and the system updates the rest from the remembered alternatives”
(doc 08-interactive). The constraint set is append-only so a session’s edit history is a
replayable log.

### Functions

| [`reoptimize`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md#equate.interactive.constraints.reoptimize)(scores[, constraints, sense])   | Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Classes

| [`ConstraintSet`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.constraints.html.md#equate.interactive.constraints.ConstraintSet)([forced, forbidden])   | Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden` (rejected) `(i, j)` edges.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.interactive.constraints.ConstraintSet(forced=list(), forbidden=list())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden`
(rejected) `(i, j)` edges.

#### confirm(i, j)

Force edge `(i, j)` into the assignment (a user-confirmed match).

#### reject(i, j)

Forbid edge `(i, j)` from the assignment (a user-rejected match).

### equate.interactive.constraints.reoptimize(scores, constraints=None, , sense='maximize')

Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).

Returns the matched `(i, j)` pairs. Raises `ValueError` if the constraints are
infeasible (no valid assignment). This is O(one LAP): the whole point is that an edit
is a cheap constrained re-solve, not a from-scratch recompute.


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md

# equate.interactive

The interactive stage: human-in-the-loop review and re-optimization.

The payoff of retaining **top-k candidates with scores** (doc 08-interactive): a user can
edit a match and the system re-solves the rest from the remembered alternatives. The pieces:

- [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) — the per-item top-k SSOT (built from a score matrix; serializable);
- [`k_best_assignments()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.k_best_assignments) — Murty’s k-best global matchings, in order (in-house, pure scipy);
- [`ConstraintSet`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.ConstraintSet) + [`reoptimize()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.reoptimize) — every edit is a force/forbid constraint,
  re-solved with one constrained LAP, not a from-scratch recompute;
- [`review_queue()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.review_queue) / [`uncertainty_sampling()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.uncertainty_sampling) — rank items by confidence margin for
  human review and active-learning query selection.

Structured explanations use [`equate.base.Explanation`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Explanation). Heavier active-learning
backends (modAL / scikit-activeml) are optional (`equate[active]`); the margin-based
query strategy here needs no extra.

### Functions

| [`k_best_assignments`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.k_best_assignments)(cost, k)                    | The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty).                          |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`solve_constrained`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.solve_constrained)(cost[, forced, forbidden])   | Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.                                              |
| [`reoptimize`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.reoptimize)(scores[, constraints, sense])       | Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).                      |
| [`review_queue`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.review_queue)(candidate_store, \*[, ...])       | Order the left items of a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) for review. |
| [`uncertainty_sampling`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.uncertainty_sampling)(candidate_store, \*[, n]) | Active-learning query: the `n` most uncertain items to label next.                                    |

### Classes

| [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore)(candidates[, sense, ...])   | Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.                      |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`ConstraintSet`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.ConstraintSet)([forced, forbidden])         | Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden` (rejected) `(i, j)` edges. |

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per left index `i`, its top-k `(right_index, score)` candidates, best-first.

Iterating yields the top-1 `(i, j)` pairs, so `dict(store)` gives the greedy 1:n
match. `row_labels` / `col_labels` name the two collections.

#### *classmethod* from_scores(scores, , k=5, sense='maximize', row_labels=None, col_labels=None)

Build a store of each row’s top-`k` candidates from a (dense or sparse) score
matrix.

A **sparse** matrix considers only its stored (candidate) cells — which is exactly
the blocking semantics (an absent cell is not a candidate), so for a blocked matrix
this intentionally differs from the dense all-cells behavior regardless of `sense`.

#### margin(i)

Confidence gap between item `i`’s top-1 and top-2 candidate scores.

A *small* margin means the top choice is uncertain (two close candidates) — the

candidates is unambiguous (no rival to be confused with), so its margin is `+inf`

### *class* equate.interactive.ConstraintSet(forced=list(), forbidden=list())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Append-only record of user edits: `forced` (confirmed) and `forbidden`
(rejected) `(i, j)` edges.

### equate.interactive.k_best_assignments(cost, k)

The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty).

Returns a list of `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` — fewer than `k` if there are
not that many feasible assignments.

```pycon
>>> [c for _, c in k_best_assignments([[1, 2], [2, 1]], 2)]
[2.0, 4.0]
```

### equate.interactive.reoptimize(scores, constraints=None, , sense='maximize')

Re-solve the optimal 1:1 assignment honoring `constraints` (confirmed/rejected).

Returns the matched `(i, j)` pairs. Raises `ValueError` if the constraints are
infeasible (no valid assignment). This is O(one LAP): the whole point is that an edit
is a cheap constrained re-solve, not a from-scratch recompute.

### equate.interactive.review_queue(candidate_store, , most_uncertain_first=True)

Order the left items of a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) for review.

By default the most-uncertain items (smallest top-1/top-2 margin) come first — the
decisions a human should look at soonest.

### equate.interactive.solve_constrained(cost, forced=(), forbidden=())

Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.

`forced` = `(i, j)` edges that MUST be in the assignment; `forbidden` = `(i, j)`
edges that must NOT. Returns `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` or `None` if the
constraints admit no valid assignment.

### equate.interactive.uncertainty_sampling(candidate_store, , n=10)

Active-learning query: the `n` most uncertain items to label next.

Uncertainty sampling — label the items whose top choice is least certain (smallest
margin), since those labels are the most informative for training a matcher.

# _autosummary/equate.interactive.kbest.html.md

# equate.interactive.kbest

k-best assignments via Murty’s algorithm (in-house; pure numpy/scipy).

Enumerating the k lowest-cost assignments *in order* is the substrate for interactive
re-optimization: retain the top-k global matchings so that when a user confirms or rejects
an edge, the next-best consistent assignment is already known (decision register D10 /
doc 08-interactive). No well-maintained pure-Python Murty exists on PyPI, so equate ships
one. `solve_constrained` (a LAP with forced / forbidden edges) is also the primitive the
interactive re-optimization uses directly.

### Functions

| [`solve_constrained`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.kbest.html.md#equate.interactive.kbest.solve_constrained)(cost[, forced, forbidden])   | Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.                     |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`k_best_assignments`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.kbest.html.md#equate.interactive.kbest.k_best_assignments)(cost, k)                    | The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty). |

### equate.interactive.kbest.k_best_assignments(cost, k)

The `k` lowest-cost assignments of `cost`, in increasing-cost order (Murty).

Returns a list of `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` — fewer than `k` if there are
not that many feasible assignments.

```pycon
>>> [c for _, c in k_best_assignments([[1, 2], [2, 1]], 2)]
[2.0, 4.0]
```

### equate.interactive.kbest.solve_constrained(cost, forced=(), forbidden=())

Minimum-cost assignment of `cost` with edge constraints.

`forced` = `(i, j)` edges that MUST be in the assignment; `forbidden` = `(i, j)`
edges that must NOT. Returns `(assignment: {i: j}, total_cost)` or `None` if the
constraints admit no valid assignment.


# _autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md

# equate.interactive.review

Human review triage and active-learning query selection.

Both rank items by *uncertainty* — the confidence margin between an item’s top-1 and top-2
candidates (small margin = an ambiguous, review-worthy decision). [`review_queue()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md#equate.interactive.review.review_queue)
orders items for a verification UI; [`uncertainty_sampling()`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md#equate.interactive.review.uncertainty_sampling) picks the most-informative
items for an oracle to label (active learning). An `Oracle` is any callable
`(i, j) -> bool` (a human, an LLM, or a crowd) — kept as a plain protocol, not a class.

| [`review_queue`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md#equate.interactive.review.review_queue)(candidate_store, \*[, ...])       | Order the left items of a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) for review.   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`uncertainty_sampling`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.review.html.md#equate.interactive.review.uncertainty_sampling)(candidate_store, \*[, n]) | Active-learning query: the `n` most uncertain items to label next.                                                                        |

Order the left items of a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore) for review.

By default the most-uncertain items (smallest top-1/top-2 margin) come first — the
decisions a human should look at soonest.

# _autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md

# equate.matching.assign

Assignment matchers (stage ③): turn a score matrix into matched `(i, j)` pairs.

Expose the *objective* (optimal / greedy / stable), not the algorithm. The optimal
matcher is **sparse-aware**: a blocked (sparse) score matrix routes to the sparse LAP
solver instead of densifying. All route similarity→cost through the `to_cost` SSOT
(decision register D2), so a `sense` of `'maximize'` (similarity) or `'minimize'`
(distance) is honored consistently.

### Functions

| [`optimal_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#equate.matching.assign.optimal_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])   | Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).              |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`greedy_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#equate.matching.assign.greedy_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])    | Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both. |
| [`stable_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#equate.matching.assign.stable_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])    | Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).          |

### equate.matching.assign.greedy_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both.

Order-dependent and not globally optimal, but fast. Iterates
[`stored_entries()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.stored_entries), so for a sparse (blocked) matrix only
the stored candidate cells are considered — an absent cell is never a match.

### equate.matching.assign.optimal_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw dense/sparse array with
`sense=` (back-compat). Solves `linear_sum_assignment` on
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) — so a **sparse (blocked)** matrix has its
absent cells worst-cased (never preferred over a real pair) and any assignment landing
on a non-candidate cell is dropped via [`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask):
a row with no candidate is left unmatched (a *partial* matching), an all-absent matrix
yields no matches. Densifying the cost is a correctness stopgap; a non-densifying
sparse LAP is a future optimization (scipy’s sparse solver silently drops
explicitly-stored zero-score candidates, so it is not used here).

### equate.matching.assign.stable_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).

See [`equate.util.stable_marriage_matching()`](_autosummary/equate.util.html.md#equate.util.stable_marriage_matching). Ranks preferences by
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) (absent cells worst-cased), so a sparse
(blocked) cell never out-ranks a real candidate; hole-assignments are then dropped via
[`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask).


# _autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md

# equate.matching.embedding_align

Embedding-based network alignment: embed both graphs’ nodes, then match the embeddings.

Two quadratic matchers (doc `12` §4) that scale past IsoRank-style propagation by
reasoning over node *embeddings* instead of the `n1 x n2` product graph, both in-house
numpy (no extra):

- `'regal'` — REGAL / xNetMF (Heimann et al., CIKM 2018): each node is described by the
  degree distribution of its k-hop neighbourhood (plus its label), the two graphs are
  embedded *jointly* through a Nyström factorization of that similarity, and nodes are
  matched by embedding similarity. Needs no correspondence to start from.
- `'cone'` — CONE-Align (Chen et al., CIKM 2020): each graph gets its own proximity
  embedding (NetMF), and the two embedding spaces are aligned by alternating an
  orthogonal Procrustes rotation with an entropic optimal-transport correspondence,
  starting from REGAL’s structural similarity (or `node_affinity`).

Both return a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) through the same flat `extract` step as
IsoRank, with the node-pair scores in `.plan`. Use them as `equate.align(G1, G2,
how='regal')` or `how='cone'`.

### Functions

| [`regal`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.regal)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...])   | Align two graphs with REGAL (xNetMF embeddings) -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching).   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`regal_scores`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.regal_scores)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, ...])   | The REGAL node-pair score matrix `exp(-||y_u - y_v||)` (`n1 x n2`).                                                                    |
| [`cone`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.cone)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...])    | Align two graphs with CONE-Align -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.    |
| [`cone_scores`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.cone_scores)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, ...])    | The CONE-Align correspondence plan (`n1 x n2`, sums to 1).                                                                             |
| [`sinkhorn_plan`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.sinkhorn_plan)(cost, \*[, reg, max_iter, tol])    | Entropic optimal-transport plan between uniform marginals (log-domain Sinkhorn).                                                       |

### equate.matching.embedding_align.cone(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, \*\*config)

Align two graphs with CONE-Align -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.

`**config` goes to [`cone_scores()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.cone_scores); `.plan` holds the final transport plan.

### equate.matching.embedding_align.cone_scores(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, dim=64, window=10, n_iter=30, reg=0.05, label=None)

The CONE-Align correspondence plan (`n1 x n2`, sums to 1).

Embeds each graph on its own (NetMF, `dim` dimensions, `window` hops), then
alternates `n_iter` times: a rotation `Q` aligning the spaces (orthogonal
Procrustes on the current correspondence) and a correspondence `P` (entropic OT,
`reg`, on the distances after rotation). It starts from `node_affinity` when given,
else from REGAL’s structural similarity. Seed rows/columns are pinned in every step.
The plan’s marginals are accurate to about `1e-4` (relative): enough to rank and
extract; [`sinkhorn_plan()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.sinkhorn_plan) is the place for a precise plan.

### equate.matching.embedding_align.regal(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, \*\*config)

Align two graphs with REGAL (xNetMF embeddings) -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching).

`**config` goes to [`regal_scores()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#equate.matching.embedding_align.regal_scores); `seeds` are kept as given.

```pycon
>>> G1 = {'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a', 'c', 'd'], 'c': ['b'], 'd': ['b', 'e'], 'e': ['d']}
>>> G2 = {1: [2, 4], 2: [1], 3: [4], 4: [1, 3, 5], 5: [4]}  # the same graph, renamed
>>> dict(regal(G1, G2).labeled_pairs())['b']
4
```

### equate.matching.embedding_align.regal_scores(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, max_hops=2, discount=0.1, gamma_struct=1.0, gamma_attr=1.0, dim=None, seed=0, label=None)

The REGAL node-pair score matrix `exp(-||y_u - y_v||)` (`n1 x n2`).

Embeddings come from xNetMF over both graphs at once (so they share a space with no
correspondence given): structural identity = degree histograms of the `max_hops`
neighbourhood, plus a label mismatch term (`label=`). `dim` sets the number of
landmarks (default `10 log2 n`); `seed` picks them reproducibly. A
`node_affinity` prior multiplies the scores.

### equate.matching.embedding_align.sinkhorn_plan(cost, , reg=0.05, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-06)

Entropic optimal-transport plan between uniform marginals (log-domain Sinkhorn).

Pure numpy (no POT): the plan `P` minimizes `<P, cost> - reg * H(P)` with rows
summing to `1/n` and columns to `1/m`. `reg` is relative to the cost’s spread,
so the same value works at any cost scale. Warns if `max_iter` runs out first.

```pycon
>>> P = sinkhorn_plan(np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]]), reg=0.01)
>>> P.round(3).tolist()
[[0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 0.5]]
```


# _autosummary/equate.matching.html.md

# equate.matching

The match stage (③): turn a score matrix into a correspondence.

A *Matcher* is a strategy over a score structure — the choice is the **objective**, not
the algorithm (decision register D4). Select by name via the [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers) registry or
pass a callable `(scores, *, sense) -> pairs`. The optimal matcher is sparse-aware
(routes a blocked matrix to the sparse LAP); soft matching (optimal transport) lives in a
parallel [`soft_match()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.soft_match) / [`harden()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.harden) seam.

### Module Attributes

| [`matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.matchers)   | the match-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`resolve_matcher`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.resolve_matcher)([spec])                          | Resolve `spec` to a runner `(scores_or_scorematrix, *, sense=None) -> pairs`.                                                    |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`optimal_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.optimal_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])            | Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).                                                                 |
| [`greedy_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.greedy_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])             | Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both.                                                    |
| [`stable_matching`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.stable_matching)(scores, \*[, sense])             | Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).                                                             |
| [`soft_match`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.soft_match)(scores, \*[, sense, reg, a, b])       | Entropic optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) plan over the cost derived from `scores`.                                                  |
| [`harden`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.harden)(plan)                                     | Recover a hard 1:1 assignment from a transport `plan` (LAP maximizing mass).                                                     |
| [`resolve_quadratic_matcher`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.resolve_quadratic_matcher)([spec])                | A registered name (built with `**config`) or a callable `(G1, G2, **kw) -> Matching`.                                            |
| [`align`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.align)(G1, G2, \*[, how, node_affinity, seeds])   | Align the nodes of two graphs -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs. |
| [`isorank`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.isorank)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...]) | Align two graphs with IsoRank -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs. |
| [`rrwm`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.rrwm)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...])    | Align two graphs with pygmtools' RRWM — requires `equate[graph-matching]`.                                                       |

### equate.matching.align(G1, G2, , how='isorank', node_affinity=None, seeds=None, \*\*config)

Align the nodes of two graphs -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.

`how` picks the quadratic matcher (`'isorank'` core, `'rrwm'` via
`equate[graph-matching]`, or a callable); `node_affinity` is an optional prior
(an `(n1, n2)` array or a `(u, v) -> float` callable, non-negative) and usually
what makes topology-only alignment work (see `isorank_scores()`); `seeds` are
known `(G1 node, G2 node)` anchors. Other keywords configure the matcher (e.g.
`extract='greedy'`, `alpha=0.9`). Graphs may be networkx graphs, `{node:
neighbors}` mappings or adjacency matrices.

```pycon
>>> star = {'hub': ['x', 'y', 'z'], 'x': ['hub'], 'y': ['hub'], 'z': ['hub']}
>>> other = {0: [3], 1: [3], 2: [3], 3: [0, 1, 2]}
>>> dict(align(star, other).labeled_pairs())['hub']
3
```

### equate.matching.greedy_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Greedy 1:1: repeatedly take the best still-available `(i, j)`, removing both.

Order-dependent and not globally optimal, but fast. Iterates
[`stored_entries()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.stored_entries), so for a sparse (blocked) matrix only
the stored candidate cells are considered — an absent cell is never a match.

### equate.matching.harden(plan)

Recover a hard 1:1 assignment from a transport `plan` (LAP maximizing mass).

### equate.matching.isorank(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, \*\*config)

Align two graphs with IsoRank -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.

`matching.labeled_pairs()` yields `(G1 node, G2 node)`; `.plan` holds the full
IsoRank score matrix. `extract` is the flat matcher that turns it into a 1:1
correspondence (any name or callable [`equate.matching.resolve_matcher()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.resolve_matcher) takes);
`**config` goes to `isorank_scores()` (`alpha`, `max_iter`, `tol`).

```pycon
>>> G1 = {'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a', 'c', 'd'], 'c': ['b'], 'd': ['b', 'e'], 'e': ['d']}
>>> G2 = {1: [2, 4], 2: [1], 3: [4], 4: [1, 3, 5], 5: [4]}  # the same graph, renamed
>>> dict(isorank(G1, G2).labeled_pairs())['b'], dict(isorank(G1, G2).labeled_pairs())['d']
(4, 1)
```

### equate.matching.matchers *= <equate.registry.Registry object>*

the match-stage strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)

### equate.matching.optimal_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Globally optimal 1:1 assignment (the linear assignment problem).

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw dense/sparse array with
`sense=` (back-compat). Solves `linear_sum_assignment` on
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) — so a **sparse (blocked)** matrix has its
absent cells worst-cased (never preferred over a real pair) and any assignment landing
on a non-candidate cell is dropped via [`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask):
a row with no candidate is left unmatched (a *partial* matching), an all-absent matrix
yields no matches. Densifying the cost is a correctness stopgap; a non-densifying
sparse LAP is a future optimization (scipy’s sparse solver silently drops
explicitly-stored zero-score candidates, so it is not used here).

### equate.matching.resolve_matcher(spec='optimal', \*\*config)

Resolve `spec` to a runner `(scores_or_scorematrix, *, sense=None) -> pairs`.

A registered name (or a facade `how=` alias like `'assign' -> 'optimal'`) is built
via the registry; a callable is used as-is. The returned runner coerces its argument to
a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) and then either hands that matrix to a **native**
matcher (so it worst-cases holes through the sanctioned views) or hands a **legacy**
raw-array matcher a hole-worst-cased dense array — so the sparse hole-worst-casing holds
no matter which contract the matcher follows (D11).

Note this returns a *runner*, not `spec` itself: unlike the pre-D11 version it is no
longer an identity passthrough for a callable (`resolve_matcher(f) is f` was true, and
is not any more). The runner carries the wrapped matcher’s `__name__`/`__doc__`, and
the original is recoverable via `__wrapped__`.

### equate.matching.resolve_quadratic_matcher(spec='isorank', \*\*config)

A registered name (built with `**config`) or a callable `(G1, G2, **kw) -> Matching`.

### equate.matching.rrwm(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, sigma=1.0, \*\*rrwm_params)

Align two graphs with pygmtools’ RRWM — requires `equate[graph-matching]`.

Builds the quadratic affinity `K` from Gaussian edge-weight agreement (bandwidth
`sigma`) with `node_affinity` on its diagonal, solves it with `pygmtools.rrwm`
(`**rrwm_params` forwarded), and extracts a 1:1 correspondence with the flat
`extract` matcher. Seeds *condition* the solve: every assignment contradicting one
(its node paired elsewhere) is removed from `K` and the seed pair gets the top
affinity, so the rest is aligned around it; seeds are then kept as given. Graphs with
no edges and no prior fall back to a uniform node affinity. Uses the numpy backend
and never changes pygmtools’ global backend.

### equate.matching.soft_match(scores, , sense=None, reg=0.1, a=None, b=None)

Entropic optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) plan over the cost derived from `scores`.

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw array with `sense=`.
Returns a dense transport-plan matrix whose rows/cols sum to the marginals `a`/`b`
(uniform by default). Requires `equate[ot]` (POT). `reg` (entropic regularization)
must be > 0 (`reg=0` divides by zero inside Sinkhorn).

### equate.matching.stable_matching(scores, , sense=None)

Gale-Shapley stable matching (optimizes stability, not total score).

See [`equate.util.stable_marriage_matching()`](_autosummary/equate.util.html.md#equate.util.stable_marriage_matching). Ranks preferences by
[`dense_cost()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.dense_cost) (absent cells worst-cased), so a sparse
(blocked) cell never out-ranks a real candidate; hole-assignments are then dropped via
[`candidate_mask()`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix.candidate_mask).

### Modules

| [`assign`](_autosummary/equate.matching.assign.html.md#module-equate.matching.assign)                   | Assignment matchers (stage ③): turn a score matrix into matched `(i, j)` pairs.                                                                                               |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`embedding_align`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#module-equate.matching.embedding_align) | Embedding-based network alignment: embed both graphs' nodes, then match the embeddings.                                                                                       |
| [`quadratic`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#module-equate.matching.quadratic)             | Quadratic matchers: align the *nodes* of two graphs (network alignment).                                                                                                      |
| [`soft`](_autosummary/equate.matching.soft.html.md#module-equate.matching.soft)                       | Soft / optimal-transport matching (stage ③): a fractional transport plan rather than a hard assignment — the home for graded, partial, unequal-mass and cross-modal matching. |


# _autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md

# equate.matching.quadratic

Quadratic matchers: align the *nodes* of two graphs (network alignment).

The second matcher arity (decision register D8, doc `12` §4). A flat matcher picks
pairs from a fixed score matrix; here how well `u` matches `v` \*depends on how their
neighbors are matched\* — a quadratic assignment problem — so the scores and the
correspondence are produced together, from the two graphs. Each quadratic matcher builds a
node-pair score matrix and hands it to a **flat** matcher (`extract=`, default the
optimal LAP) for the final 1:1 correspondence.

- `'isorank'` (core) — IsoRank (Singh, Xu & Berger 2008): “two nodes match if their
  neighbors match”, the stationary point of a random walk on the product graph, blended
  with an optional prior `node_affinity`.
- `'final'` (core) — FINAL (Zhang & Tong 2016): IsoRank’s propagation gated by node
  attribute agreement (`label=` / `attribute_similarity=`).
- `'regal'`, `'cone'` (core, [`equate.matching.embedding_align`](_autosummary/equate.matching.embedding_align.html.md#module-equate.matching.embedding_align)) — embedding
  aligners: REGAL/xNetMF (joint structural embeddings) and CONE-Align (per-graph NetMF
  embeddings aligned by Procrustes + optimal transport).
- `'gw'` (`equate[ot]`) — Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport on shortest-path
  distances (fused with `node_affinity` when given); `.plan` is the transport plan.
- `'rrwm'` (`equate[graph-matching]`) — pygmtools’ reweighted random walk solver on
  the full quadratic affinity (edge-weight agreement + `node_affinity`).

PLANETALIGN is not wrapped: it has no PyPI distribution, and the in-house aligners above
cover its core methods (a git-sourced backend can register here later as another entry).

Use [`align()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.align) (also `equate.align`), or pick a strategy from the
[`quadratic_matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.quadratic_matchers) registry. `seeds` are known node correspondences
(anchors): they are kept as given and steer the rest.

### Module Attributes

| [`DFLT_ISORANK_ALPHA`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.DFLT_ISORANK_ALPHA)   | weight of the topology term vs the `node_affinity` prior (1 = topology only).   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`DFLT_EDGE_SIGMA`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.DFLT_EDGE_SIGMA)      | bandwidth of the Gaussian edge-weight agreement used by `'rrwm'`.               |
| [`quadratic_matchers`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.quadratic_matchers)   | the quadratic-matcher strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)                  |

### Functions

| [`resolve_quadratic_matcher`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.resolve_quadratic_matcher)([spec])                | A registered name (built with `**config`) or a callable `(G1, G2, **kw) -> Matching`.                                            |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`align`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.align)(G1, G2, \*[, how, node_affinity, seeds])   | Align the nodes of two graphs -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs. |
| [`isorank`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.isorank)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...]) | Align two graphs with IsoRank -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs. |
| [`isorank_scores`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.isorank_scores)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, ...]) | The IsoRank node-pair score matrix `R` (`n1 x n2`, sums to 1).                                                                   |
| [`rrwm`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.rrwm)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...])    | Align two graphs with pygmtools' RRWM — requires `equate[graph-matching]`.                                                       |
| [`final`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.final)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...])   | Align two graphs with FINAL -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.   |
| [`final_scores`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.final_scores)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, ...])   | The FINAL node-pair score matrix (Zhang & Tong, KDD 2016; the FINAL-N variant).                                                  |
| [`gw`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.gw)(G1, G2, \*[, node_affinity, seeds, ...])      | Align two graphs by Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport — `equate[ot]` (POT).                                                   |

### equate.matching.quadratic.DFLT_EDGE_SIGMA *= 1.0*

bandwidth of the Gaussian edge-weight agreement used by `'rrwm'`.

### equate.matching.quadratic.DFLT_ISORANK_ALPHA *= 0.8*

weight of the topology term vs the `node_affinity` prior (1 = topology only).

### equate.matching.quadratic.align(G1, G2, , how='isorank', node_affinity=None, seeds=None, \*\*config)

Align the nodes of two graphs -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.

`how` picks the quadratic matcher (`'isorank'` core, `'rrwm'` via
`equate[graph-matching]`, or a callable); `node_affinity` is an optional prior
(an `(n1, n2)` array or a `(u, v) -> float` callable, non-negative) and usually
what makes topology-only alignment work (see [`isorank_scores()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.isorank_scores)); `seeds` are
known `(G1 node, G2 node)` anchors. Other keywords configure the matcher (e.g.
`extract='greedy'`, `alpha=0.9`). Graphs may be networkx graphs, `{node:
neighbors}` mappings or adjacency matrices.

```pycon
>>> star = {'hub': ['x', 'y', 'z'], 'x': ['hub'], 'y': ['hub'], 'z': ['hub']}
>>> other = {0: [3], 1: [3], 2: [3], 3: [0, 1, 2]}
>>> dict(align(star, other).labeled_pairs())['hub']
3
```

### equate.matching.quadratic.final(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, \*\*config)

Align two graphs with FINAL -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.

Like [`isorank()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.isorank), with node attributes (`label=` or `attribute_similarity=`)
gating the propagation; `**config` goes to [`final_scores()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.final_scores).

```pycon
>>> G1 = {'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a', 'c'], 'c': ['b']}
>>> G2 = {1: [2], 2: [1, 3], 3: [2]}
>>> kinds = {'a': 'x', 'b': 'y', 'c': 'z', 1: 'z', 2: 'y', 3: 'x'}
>>> dict(final(G1, G2, label=kinds.get).labeled_pairs())
{'a': 3, 'b': 2, 'c': 1}
```

### equate.matching.quadratic.final_scores(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, attribute_similarity=None, alpha=0.8, max_iter=100, tol=1e-09, label=None)

The FINAL node-pair score matrix (Zhang & Tong, KDD 2016; the FINAL-N variant).

IsoRank’s “two nodes match if their neighbors match”, with every step of the walk on
the product graph filtered by **node-attribute agreement** `N` (from `label=`, or
`attribute_similarity`) and symmetrically degree-normalized:
`X <- alpha * N * D^-1/2 (A1 (N * D^-1/2 * X) A2^T) + (1 - alpha) * H`, `H` the
normalized prior (`node_affinity`, seeds pinned as in IsoRank). Without attributes
(`N` all ones) it reduces to IsoRank-style propagation. Returned as a
`ScoreMatrix` (`sense='maximize'`).

### equate.matching.quadratic.gw(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, alpha=0.5, \*\*gw_params)

Align two graphs by Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport — `equate[ot]` (POT).

GW finds the coupling of the two node sets that best preserves *distances*: nodes
far apart in `G1` should map to nodes far apart in `G2` (shortest-path lengths,
scaled to `[0, 1]`). With a `node_affinity` (or `seeds`) it is *fused* GW: a
node-feature cost `1 - affinity/max` weighted `1 - alpha` against the structure
(`alpha`). `.plan` holds the transport plan, the soft correspondence; `extract`
hardens it. `**gw_params` go to POT (`max_iter`, `tol_rel`, …); options that
change POT’s return type (`log`) are refused.

### equate.matching.quadratic.isorank(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, \*\*config)

Align two graphs with IsoRank -> a [`Matching`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Matching) of node pairs.

`matching.labeled_pairs()` yields `(G1 node, G2 node)`; `.plan` holds the full
IsoRank score matrix. `extract` is the flat matcher that turns it into a 1:1
correspondence (any name or callable [`equate.matching.resolve_matcher()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.html.md#equate.matching.resolve_matcher) takes);
`**config` goes to [`isorank_scores()`](_autosummary/equate.matching.quadratic.html.md#equate.matching.quadratic.isorank_scores) (`alpha`, `max_iter`, `tol`).

```pycon
>>> G1 = {'a': ['b'], 'b': ['a', 'c', 'd'], 'c': ['b'], 'd': ['b', 'e'], 'e': ['d']}
>>> G2 = {1: [2, 4], 2: [1], 3: [4], 4: [1, 3, 5], 5: [4]}  # the same graph, renamed
>>> dict(isorank(G1, G2).labeled_pairs())['b'], dict(isorank(G1, G2).labeled_pairs())['d']
(4, 1)
```

### equate.matching.quadratic.isorank_scores(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, alpha=0.8, max_iter=100, tol=1e-09, label=None)

The IsoRank node-pair score matrix `R` (`n1 x n2`, sums to 1).

Iterates `R <- alpha * W1 R W2^T + (1 - alpha) * E` to its fixed point, where
`W` is each graph’s column-stochastic walk matrix and `E` the normalized prior
(`node_affinity`; uniform when `None`). `seeds` pin their rows/columns of the
prior to the given partner (at the prior’s own top value), so their anchoring
propagates to the neighbors. A directed graph walks *against* its edges (the column
normalization uses in-degrees). Warns when `max_iter` runs out before `tol`.
Returned as a `ScoreMatrix` (`sense='maximize'`) labeled with the two node lists.

The prior does real work: from topology alone (`node_affinity=None`) the scores
tend to the product of node degrees, which cannot tell equal-degree nodes apart. Pass
a node similarity (attributes, names, degrees) for anything but degree-distinct graphs.

### equate.matching.quadratic.quadratic_matchers *= <equate.registry.Registry object>*

the quadratic-matcher strategy registry (name -> lazy factory)

### equate.matching.quadratic.resolve_quadratic_matcher(spec='isorank', \*\*config)

A registered name (built with `**config`) or a callable `(G1, G2, **kw) -> Matching`.

### equate.matching.quadratic.rrwm(G1, G2, , node_affinity=None, seeds=None, extract='optimal', label=None, sigma=1.0, \*\*rrwm_params)

Align two graphs with pygmtools’ RRWM — requires `equate[graph-matching]`.

Builds the quadratic affinity `K` from Gaussian edge-weight agreement (bandwidth
`sigma`) with `node_affinity` on its diagonal, solves it with `pygmtools.rrwm`
(`**rrwm_params` forwarded), and extracts a 1:1 correspondence with the flat
`extract` matcher. Seeds *condition* the solve: every assignment contradicting one
(its node paired elsewhere) is removed from `K` and the seed pair gets the top
affinity, so the rest is aligned around it; seeds are then kept as given. Graphs with
no edges and no prior fall back to a uniform node affinity. Uses the numpy backend
and never changes pygmtools’ global backend.


# _autosummary/equate.matching.soft.html.md

# equate.matching.soft

Soft / optimal-transport matching (stage ③): a fractional transport plan rather than a
hard assignment — the home for graded, partial, unequal-mass and cross-modal matching.
Requires `equate[ot]`. Its structured siblings return plans too (decision register D8):
Gromov-Wasserstein couples two *graphs* (`equate.align(G1, G2, how='gw')`, `.plan`),
and soft-DTW couples the *elements* of two sequences
(`equate.compare.sequence.soft_dtw_alignment`).

### Functions

| [`soft_match`](_autosummary/equate.matching.soft.html.md#equate.matching.soft.soft_match)(scores, \*[, sense, reg, a, b])   | Entropic optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) plan over the cost derived from `scores`.   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`harden`](_autosummary/equate.matching.soft.html.md#equate.matching.soft.harden)(plan)                                 | Recover a hard 1:1 assignment from a transport `plan` (LAP maximizing mass).      |

### equate.matching.soft.harden(plan)

Recover a hard 1:1 assignment from a transport `plan` (LAP maximizing mass).

### equate.matching.soft.soft_match(scores, , sense=None, reg=0.1, a=None, b=None)

Entropic optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) plan over the cost derived from `scores`.

Accepts a [`ScoreMatrix`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.ScoreMatrix) (native) or a raw array with `sense=`.
Returns a dense transport-plan matrix whose rows/cols sum to the marginals `a`/`b`
(uniform by default). Requires `equate[ot]` (POT). `reg` (entropic regularization)
must be > 0 (`reg=0` divides by zero inside Sinkhorn).


# _autosummary/equate.registry.html.md

# equate.registry

A tiny name-keyed strategy registry with lazy factories (open-closed dispatch).

Each pipeline stage (featurize, compare, block, match, cluster) owns a `Registry`
mapping a string `name` to a lazy factory that builds the strategy on demand, so a
heavy optional import fires only when that strategy is actually used. Users select a
strategy by name (`featurize='tfidf'`) or pass a callable directly — [`Registry.resolve()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.resolve)
accepts both, and users can register their own strategies without subclassing.

### Classes

| [`Registry`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry)(kind)   | A `name -> lazy factory` registry for one pipeline stage's strategies.   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Exceptions

| [`UnknownStrategyError`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.UnknownStrategyError)   | No strategy is registered under that name (a `KeyError`, for back-compat).   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* equate.registry.Registry(kind)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A `name -> lazy factory` registry for one pipeline stage’s strategies.

```pycon
>>> reg = Registry('demo')
>>> @reg.register('double')
... def _double_factory():
...     return lambda x: x * 2
>>> reg.names()
['double']
>>> reg.create('double')(21)          # look up + build + call
42
>>> reg.resolve(str.upper)('hi')       # a callable passes through unchanged
'HI'
>>> 'double' in reg
True
```

#### create(name, \*args, \*\*kwargs)

Build the strategy registered under `name` (calls its lazy factory).

#### factory(name)

Return the (uncalled) factory registered under `name`.

* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)

#### meta(name)

Return the declared metadata for `name` (`None` if none was declared).

Raises `KeyError` for an unknown name, consistent with [`factory()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.factory) — so
an unknown name is never silently conflated with a known name that has no meta.

* **Return type:**
  [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)

#### names()

Sorted list of registered strategy names.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)

#### register(name, factory=None, , meta=None)

Register `factory` under `name`. Usable as a decorator or directly.

The factory is called lazily (by [`create()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.create)/[`resolve()`](_autosummary/equate.registry.html.md#equate.registry.Registry.resolve)), so any heavy
import inside it fires only on use. `meta` is optional declared metadata
(e.g. a `FeaturizerMeta`/`ComparatorMeta`).

#### resolve(spec, \*args, \*\*kwargs)

Resolve `spec` to a strategy.

A callable `spec` passes through unchanged; a `str` is looked up and its
factory is called with `(*args, **kwargs)`.

### *exception* equate.registry.UnknownStrategyError

Bases: [`KeyError`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#KeyError)

No strategy is registered under that name (a `KeyError`, for back-compat).

Its own type lets a surface tell a caller’s unknown name (an HTTP 422) from a
`KeyError` raised by a bug.


# _autosummary/equate.service.html.md

# equate.service

The service layer: equate’s matching core as JSON-in/JSON-out operations.

This module is the **surface-free** half of the HTTP service (doc 10 §5, decision D10).
Every operation is a plain method taking JSON-able arguments and returning a dataclass of
JSON-able fields, so any surface can project it: [`mk_app()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.mk_app) mounts it as an HTTP API
with `qh` (`pip install 'equate[service]'`), and the review UI in `ui/` consumes the
same payloads through Zod schemas generated from [`json_schemas()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.json_schemas).

Two kinds of operation:

- **stateless** — [`MatchService.match()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.MatchService.match): two collections in, scored pairs out (the
  batch core, cached by content);
- **session-scoped** — the interactive loop of doc 08. [`MatchService.open_session()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.MatchService.open_session)
  scores the two collections *once* and keeps a [`CandidateStore`](_autosummary/equate.interactive.html.md#equate.interactive.CandidateStore)
  of top-k candidates; [`candidates()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.MatchService.candidates) reads (or refreshes) one item’s
  top-k; [`edit()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.MatchService.edit) applies confirm / reject / reassign edits and returns
  the locally re-optimized assignment (one constrained LAP over the cached scores, never a
  re-score); [`label()`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.MatchService.label) is the active-learning `Oracle` endpoint: it
  records a human/LLM/crowd label and returns the next most-informative query.

Every response carries an [`Accounting`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.Accounting) of the time and item counts each tier
(`score`, `match`, `reoptimize`, …) cost, so a caller can budget expensive
cascades (doc 06). Sessions live in any `MutableMapping` (`sessions=`), so a
persistent `dol` store replaces the in-memory dict without touching this code.

```pycon
>>> svc = MatchService()
>>> result = svc.match(['apple pie', 'banana split'], ['banana splitt', 'aple pie'])
>>> [(p.left, p.right) for p in result.pairs]
[('apple pie', 'aple pie'), ('banana split', 'banana splitt')]
```

### Functions

| [`explain_pair`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.explain_pair)(left, right, score, \*[, ...])   | A structured [`Explanation`](_autosummary/equate.base.html.md#equate.base.Explanation) of a pair: a per-field diff.   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`record_text`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.record_text)(obj)                              | Text of `obj`: a mapping's non-empty values joined by spaces, else `str(obj)`.                                                   |
| [`to_jsonable`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.to_jsonable)(obj)                              | Convert a boundary dataclass (or nested containers of them) to plain JSON data.                                                  |
| [`json_schemas`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.json_schemas)()                                | JSON Schemas of the boundary types, keyed by type name.                                                                          |
| [`mk_app`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.mk_app)([service, cors_origins, ui_dir, ...])  | Mount a [`MatchService`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.MatchService) as an HTTP API (FastAPI, built with `qh`).                 |
| [`serve`](_autosummary/equate.service.html.md#equate.service.serve)(\*[, host, port, service, ui_dir])      | Run the HTTP service with uvicorn (`python -m equate.service serve`).                                                            |

### Classes

### *class* equate.service.CandidateView(candidate, right, score, explanation=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

### *class* equate.service.Edit(action, item, candidate, source='human')

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

One user edit of the assignment.

- `confirm` — force `item -> candidate` (a confirmed match);
- `reject` — forbid `item -> candidate`;
- `reassign` — confirm a *different* candidate for `item` (its previous forced
  match, and any other item forced onto `candidate`, are released);
- `clear` — drop any constraint on `item -> candidate` (undo).

`item` indexes the left collection, `candidate` the right one; `source` says who
made the edit (`'human'`, `'llm'`, …) — provenance for a later precedence policy.

### *class* equate.service.EditResult(session_id, assignment, changed, accounting)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

The result of an edit: the re-optimized assignment and what it changed.

`changed` lists the items whose match moved, so a UI re-renders only that block.
